    printf 'code %d\ndata %d\nbss %d\nimage %d\nstack %d\nirq_stack %d\nram_code %d\n' \
        $((data_load - origin + ram_code)) $((data - ram_code)) "$bss" $((data_load - origin + data)) \
        "$stack" "$irq" "$ram_code"
}

# The Plaits demo's own sources and the vendored Plaits (M4b,
# docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md): our C glue and runtime with the firmware's flags;
# our C++ with the same warnings, as errors (Plaits' headers are system
# headers to it: their warnings are not ours to fix); the vendored files
# unmodified at upstream's -O2, with warnings off. All the C++ is built in
# upstream's portable configuration (-DTEST), with our standard headers
# and plaits_pre.h in place of a C library's. Objects are named after their
# paths, since vendored names repeat.
build_demo_plaits() {
    d=firmware/demos/plaits
    CXX="clang -target pi32v2 -x c++ -std=c++11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -fno-exceptions
         -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics -fno-common -g -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
         -I$d/include -isystem vendor/plaits/eurorack -isystem vendor/plaits -I$d -Ifirmware/src
         -DTEST -include $d/include/plaits_pre.h"
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CXX="$CXX -D$d2"; done
    # PLAITS_HWFLOAT: the toolchain's hardware single-precision float
    # instructions (its fprev1 feature) instead of our soft-float, for the
    # C++ only: a measurement of what they would save, never the demo's
    # default, since whether the chip has them is open (SR-5).
    case " ${SB_DEFINES:-} " in
        *" PLAITS_HWFLOAT "*) CXX="$CXX -Xclang -target-feature -Xclang +fprev1" ;;
    esac
    defs=""
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do defs="$defs -D$d2"; done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS $defs -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2046
            *) set -x; clang $(echo "$CFLAGS" | sed 's/ -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1//') -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        set -x; $CXX -Os -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        $CXX -O2 -w -c "$s" -o "$o"
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    echo "built $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | wc -l) vendored Plaits files"
}

cmd_inside() {
    src=$1 out=$2
    cd "$src"
    # The chip's CPU model and its single-precision float instructions, as
    # the SDK builds for it (HW-62, since M5). The Plaits demo's own C is
    # built without them, as before (build_demo_plaits): its soft-float
    # test must exercise the soft-float routines, and `-mcpu=r3` on its
    # own already makes the compiler use the instructions.
    CPU="-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1"
    # -nostdinc: no C library headers either; the SDK's register headers
    # are the only outside includes. -fno-common puts zeroed data in .bss.
    CFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -Os -g
            -fno-common -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
            -Ifirmware/src -Ivendor/jieli-sdk/include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -D$d"; done
    # Assembly is built without -g, which would record the source path.
    ASFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -nostdinc -Werror"
    clang --version | head -1
    ld --version | head -1
    echo "SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH"
    # Objects are intermediate: kept out of the outputs.
    obj=/tmp/small-beeps-obj
    rm -rf "$obj" && mkdir -p "$obj"
    objs=""
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -DSB_DEMO_PLAITS -Ifirmware/demos/plaits"
    fi
    for s in $(find firmware/src -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(basename "$s" | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *) set -x; clang $CFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        build_demo_plaits
    fi
    set -x
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    ld -nostdlib --no-undefined --orphan-handling=error -T firmware/app.ld \
        -o "$out/app.elf" $objs
    # The raw image is the code, then the initial data, which app.ld loads
    # right after it. This objcopy takes one section at a time, and ld's
    # own binary output gets data addresses wrong, so the two are joined.
    objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/app.elf" "$obj/text.bin"
    objcopy -O binary -j .data "$out/app.elf" "$obj/data.bin"
    cat "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin" > "$out/app.bin"
    # The package link (Phase A1, HW-91): the same objects, linked where a
    # package's app.bin runs, 0x120 past the window's start; its raw image
    # is what tools/fwsc.py packs into a .fwsc. Not for a demo.
    if [ -z "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        ld -nostdlib --no-undefined --orphan-handling=error --defsym=IMAGE_ORIGIN=0x02000120 \
            -T firmware/app.ld -o "$out/app-pkg.elf" $objs
        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/app-pkg.elf" "$obj/pkg-text.bin"
        objcopy -O binary -j .data "$out/app-pkg.elf" "$obj/pkg-data.bin"
        cat "$obj/pkg-text.bin" "$obj/pkg-data.bin" > "$out/app-pkg.bin"
    fi
    set +x
    write_size "$out/app.elf" > "$out/app.size"
    cat "$out/app.size"
    image=$(awk '$1 == "image" { print $2 }' "$out/app.size")
    if [ "$(wc -c < "$out/app.bin")" -ne "$image" ]; then
        echo "FAIL: app.bin is not the $image bytes app.ld lays out" >&2; exit 1
    fi
    # Nothing in the firmware may depend on which link it is (A1-1): what
    # runs from RAM is byte for byte the same in both, the boot code (run
    # from the window) is as long, and the package's starts at 0x02000120.
    # The RAM check is the firmware's, not a test build's: the store's wipe
    # test (SB_TEST_STORE_WIPE) turns a link symbol into a chip offset.
    if [ -z "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        [ -n "${SB_DEFINES:-}" ] || cmp "$obj/data.bin" "$obj/pkg-data.bin" \
            || { echo "FAIL: the package link's RAM code and data differ from the raw image's" >&2; exit 1; }
        [ "$(wc -c < "$obj/pkg-text.bin")" -eq "$(wc -c < "$obj/text.bin")" ] \
            || { echo "FAIL: the package link's boot code is not as long as the raw image's" >&2; exit 1; }
        [ "$(nm "$out/app-pkg.elf" | awk '$3 == "_start" { print $1 }')" = 02000120 ] \
            || { echo "FAIL: the package link's _start is not at 0x02000120" >&2; exit 1; }
        rm "$obj/pkg-text.bin" "$obj/pkg-data.bin"
    fi
    rm "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin"
    # No output may contain the absolute source path.
    for f in $(find "$out" -type f | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        if grep -q -F "$src" "$f"; then
            echo "FAIL: $f contains the source path $src" >&2; exit 1
        fi
    done
    (cd "$out" && find . -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS | sed 's|^\./||' \
        | LC_ALL=C sort | xargs sha256sum > SHA256SUMS)
}

case "${1:-}" in
    image) cmd_image ;;
    image-tag) image_tag ;;
    build) shift; cmd_build "$@" ;;
    inside) shift; cmd_inside "$@" ;;
    *) sed -n '5,12p' "$0" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""The timing goldens' policy (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, "Timing goldens"),
for the suites that compare fwtest's outputs with golden files.

A bigger or slower image starts a few microseconds later, and every
event of the firmware's that waits on an audio block can then move by a
block (1.451 ms) or by a MIDI byte (0.320 ms). The rules:

1. A run's end clears the audio blocks: the end asked for (--ms) falls
   at least END_BEFORE_MS before the next block's end and at least
   END_AFTER_MS after the last one. An end comes late, never early, while
   core 0 waits (docs/HARNESS.md, "Time"), and start-up only moves the
   blocks later, so the margins say how far either can go before the run
   takes one block more or less (check_end, from the run's ipb.csv).
2. MIDI out's captures are compared with a stated tolerance: the same
   bytes in the same order (the same messages, decoded), each at its

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""Runs the firmware's fwtest suite and checks what it captured (check
C-FW-SUITE; R-BOOT-1 to R-BOOT-5, R-CLK-1, R-IRQ-1 to R-IRQ-4, R-LCD-1
to R-LCD-5, and since M3 R-KEY-1 to R-KEY-3, R-ENC-1, R-ENC-2, R-POT-1,
R-POT-2, R-LED-1 to R-LED-3, R-INPUT-1 to R-INPUT-3).

  fw-suite.py --build DIR --out DIR

Copies DIR/app.bin (a tools/build.sh output) to out/fw/app.bin and builds
the test images (TEST_BUILDS: the same source with one SB_TEST_* define
each) to out/fw/<name>.bin, where tests/fw/boot.suite expects them, runs
the suite through tools/fwtest (the pinned image), and then checks:

- every case: the outcome the suite expects, no unmodelled accesses
  (until M5 also that core 1 never ran: since M5 it runs the FM engine);
- boot: the marker; the vector table, every slot (HW-18): source 4 is
  sb_tick, source 16 lcd_spi_done, source 5 input_scan (since M3), every
  other source its own stub in crt0.S, by the ELF's
  symbols; the clock measured at startup: SB_CLOCK_CYCLES core cycles take
  CLOCK_TICKS time base ticks (240 MHz against 24 MHz, HW-11, HW-13); the
  first tick within FIRST_TICK_MS of the start (from the last tick's time
  base, the ticks taken and the shortest interval, since the run itself
  ends late); nothing halted;
- heartbeat (one emulated second; the image idles between ticks, so
  captures come late, docs/HARNESS.md "Time"): at every capture at least
  one of the beacon's two heartbeat copies is consistent, beats ==
  ticks // 24000, and both are when its seq is even (the tick handler
  writes them in turn, DESIGN-NOTES.md M1); the consistent copy's ticks
  are no earlier than the time asked less one tick period and START_SLACK,
  and no more than LATE_MS after it; beats never go back. At the end:
  the last tick's time base lies within one tick period (and START_SLACK)
  before fwtest's emulated end time; every interval between two ticks is
  within INTERVAL_TOL of 24 000 time base ticks (1 ms), and so is their
  spread (jitter); beats and ticks taken differ by at most one; the idle
  wait returned at least once per tick and (since M3) at most once per
  interrupt, and core 0 ran at most IDLE_MAX_IPT instructions per tick
  (M0's polling heartbeat: M0_IPP per period);
- fault and stray: the halt recorded in the beacon (reason and source),
  and the console line, by golden file;
- badinsn: fwtest's own fault outcome for an undecodable instruction. A
  limit of the harness, not firmware behaviour: no handler of ours runs
  (SR-1).
- heartbeat2 (since M2): the heartbeat's checks again over 2.25 s; with
  heartbeat (1.25 s) its difference is the steady state, which may take
  at most IDLE_MAX_IPT instructions a tick. The idle loop's wakes, stored
  once a second, equal the ticks taken since it began, within one.
- screen (since M2): every pixel of the address pattern (300 ms) against
  its formula; the test screen's border, corners and ramps pixel by pixel
  (800 ms); one heartbeat later (1 500 ms) only the heartbeat's rows
  changed; the beacon's screen and seconds shown at each capture; and the
  three pictures against golden images.
- flood (since M2): a test build that sends whole frames back to back from
  500 ms: every tick interval still within INTERVAL_TOL, far more frames
  than ticks, and the picture still the test screen. Prints how long a
  whole frame takes.

- since M3, the panel (tests/fw/scripts/; docs/REQUIREMENTS.md has the
  limits): the input record after the beacon holds the counters, each
  control's value and the last 128 events, each stamped in time base ticks
  from when main started the time base. Each case's events (control, kind,
  value, never times) are compared with tests/fw/events/<case>.txt, and
  written as events.txt beside its outputs. Latencies run from the
  script's time of a change to the event's stamp, allowing for the time
  base starting anywhere within START_SLACK. keys: every key and button
  alone gives control n for fwtest key n, press and release, within
  KEY_LATENCY; its LED lit while held and dark otherwise (leds.csv), set
  within LED_LAG_MS of its event (the firmware's own measure). chords: no ghost, chatter and a glitch
  debounced, encoders exact with keys held in their columns, the panel
  screen against its golden image. encoders: slow detents within
  ENC_LATENCY, exact positions after fast, shared-column and all-at-once
  turns, and every tick interval within INTERVAL_TOL meanwhile. pot:
  steps within POT_FIRST and POT_SETTLED, one way each, no events at rest
  with noise, a rising sweep to 1023. leds (a test build): every LED at its
  brightness step within LED_STEP_TOL. ledshow (a test build, the keys
  script): from input_led to the scan first driving that LED, within
  LED_SHOW_MS (one scan).

- since M7, the store's cases (R-STORE-1 to R-STORE-9): runs chained
  through the flash fwtest saves, by tools/store_suite.py after the
  suite (its docstring says what each checks);

- since M5, the FM engine (tests/fw/scripts/fm*.txt; R-FM-*; the engine's
  record follows the audio record; the test patches' values come from
  tools/fm_patch.py): fmbessel, test patch 1's sidebands against
  |J_n(pi/2)| by a least-squares fit at the known frequencies; fmenv,
  test patch 2's stages (each end where its fitted line meets its level,
  its rate, the held level, the attack's linearity, no click); fmmono,
  legato and glide (one sound, one note, the pitch along the glide, no
  new attack); fmsteal, 17 notes on 16 voices, one stolen with no click;
  fmvel, the velocity test build's levels; fmgold and fmgold2, every test
  patch against a golden WAV, twice, the same bytes. audioload is the
  heaviest input on all 16 voices, and checks that core 1 renders. The
  notes case plays test patch 0.

- since M6b, MIDI out (R-MIDIOUT-*; the record at 0x01c00734, fwtest's
  --midi-out): in every case the wire's timing, one run of bytes per
  transfer of at most MIDI_OUT_CHUNK, whole messages, and a status after
  the wire went quiet (midi_out_common); midiout's messages against its
  script; midiround (midiout's golden capture into MIDI in) ends with
  midiout's engine state and pitches; midithru passes on every message
  but the SysEx, in order; midilocal plays nothing from the panel while
  local control is off; midiburst's policy leaves no note on unended;
  midioutlat's key-to-wire latency within MIDI_OUT_LATENCY_MS;
  presetends: PRESETS stops at the ends (no program change, no note
  cut, past either end).

Prints what it saw for the record, and exits 1 if anything failed.
"""
import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import math
import os
import re
import shutil
import struct
import subprocess

## Running it

The firmware side runs fwtest only through `tools/fwtest`, which runs the
published container image pinned by digest in `config/fwtest-image`
(R-SEP-3). It needs Docker; the image runs as linux/amd64 on any host.

```sh
tools/fwtest run out/build/app.bin --ms 100 --out out/t1 --ram 0x01c00000:64@end
tools/fwtest suite tests/fw/boot.suite --out out/suite
tools/fwtest version
tools/fwtest --image        # the pinned image reference
```

- Run it from the repository root. The current folder is mounted read-only,
  so every input path (image, script, flash file, golden folder, suite) must
  be inside it. `--out` is created and mounted writable on its own, and must
  be empty or not exist yet.
- The container has no network and runs as your user.
- After a run, `tools/fwtest` adds `runner.txt` to the output folder, naming
  the image it ran and whether it was the pinned one. A test record that
  used fwtest names that image; every record also notes the pinned image in
  its environment.

## The flash chip

Since 0.6.0 fwtest's flash chip behaves as the P25Q80H's datasheet says
(`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-77, HW-78, HW-83), at its maximum times:

- **Busy times.** A page program keeps the chip busy for 3 ms and an
  erase (a 256-byte page, 4 KiB, 32 KiB, 64 KiB or the whole chip) for
  12 ms, from the moment chip select goes high. Meanwhile status register
  1 reads bit 0 (busy) and bit 1 (write enable) set, and the chip ignores
  every command but the status reads, the array and ID reads too.
- **Command rules.** An erase or program needs the write enable command
  first, or it is ignored. A program wraps within its 256-byte page and
  only clears bits.
- **The code window while busy.** While the chip is busy, a core that is
  about to run code in the code window (the image, or the chip past it),
  or reads it, ends the run as a fault: "ran code in the code window
  while the flash chip was busy (an erase or program in progress)", or
  "read the code window at ADDR while ...". That includes an interrupt
  handler in the window, and core 1. So the code that erases or
  programs, and waits, runs in RAM; so does any handler that can run
  meanwhile, with everything it calls and reads; or interrupts stay
  masked. fwtest checks only while the chip is busy: on the chip the
  window is unavailable for the whole time the firmware works the flash
  directly (HW-79), from its first command. Core 1 is checked on core
  0's clock, which it trails by at most one run call (1024 instructions).
  The audio output plays on through a busy time: it reads RAM.
- **Persistence.** The chip lasts from one run to the next only through
  files: `--flash FILE` starts a run from a saved chip (the image is
  written at `0x4000` again), `--flash-out` saves it at the end, whatever
  the outcome. Give one run's `flash.bin` to the next as `--flash`.
- **A power cut.** `--power-cut MS` ends the run at MS (in place of
  `--ms`) as if the power went then, and saves `flash.bin`. An erase or
  program in progress keeps only the part done by then: its first bytes,
  in address order, in proportion to the time gone (a 4 KiB erase cut a
  quarter of the way through has its first 1 KiB erased and the rest as
  before). That is fwtest's choice: on the chip an interrupted erase or
  program leaves those bytes undefined, so a firmware must be able to
  tell an interrupted write from a finished one (a check sum, or a marker
  written last). `--flash-log` lists every erase and program with its
  times, to aim a cut. A run that ends any other way (`--ms`, a halt, a
  fault) during an erase or program saves `flash.bin` (with
  `--flash-out`) as if that operation had finished: the bytes change when
  it starts. Use `--power-cut` for a cut.

## The command line

```
fwtest run IMAGE --ms MS --out DIR [options]
fwtest run PACKAGE --package --ms MS --out DIR [options]
fwtest suite FILE --out DIR
fwtest version
```

`run` options:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--package` | The input is an update package, not a raw image ("Packages"). |
| `--ms MS` | Run for MS emulated milliseconds (up to three decimals). Required, unless `--power-cut` is given. |
| `--power-cut MS` | Run for MS emulated milliseconds, then end as a power cut: the flash keeps only the part done of an erase or program in progress, and `flash.bin` is saved ("The flash chip"). In place of `--ms`. |
| `--out DIR` | Write the outputs here. Required; must be empty or new. |
| `--script FILE` | Timed inputs (below). |
| `--flash FILE` | The flash chip's first bytes (at most 1 MiB); the rest is erased. |
| `--ram ADDR:LEN@WHEN` | Save LEN bytes of memory at ADDR at WHEN. Numbers in decimal, or hex with `0x`. Only RAM (main RAM and the other RAM banks `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` lists) can be saved; anything else is a usage error. Repeatable. |
| `--lcd WHEN` | Save the screen as a PNG at WHEN. Repeatable. |
| `--leds-every MS` | Sample the LEDs every MS into `leds.csv`. |
| `--flash-out` | Save the whole flash chip at the end (`flash.bin`). |
| `--flash-log` | Save every erase and program the chip started (`flash-ops.csv`). |
| `--wav` | Save the audio output (`audio.wav`). |
| `--ipb` | Save instructions per audio block (`ipb.csv`). |
| `--console` | Save the bytes written to the chip's debug message register (`console.txt`; `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` names it). |
| `--midi-out` | Save the MIDI output: the bytes with their times (`midi-out.csv`) and the messages they make (`midi-out.txt`). See "MIDI output". |
| `--watchdog ADDR:MS` | A hang if the 32-bit word at RAM address ADDR stays the same for more than MS ms. |
| `--halt-ok` | A halt counts as success (exit 0). |
| `--golden DIR` | Compare the outputs with the golden files in DIR (below). |

WHEN is a time in ms (`10`, `2.5`) or `end`. The run ends at `--ms`, or
earlier on a fault, halt or hang; `end` captures are taken then.

## Input scripts

A text file, one event per line; `#` starts a comment. Times are emulated
milliseconds with up to three decimals. Events at the same time happen in
the order written.

```
# time   event
2        key 12 down
4        key 12 up
6        key 5 tap 3          # down at 6 ms, up at 9 ms (default hold: 50 ms)
10       enc 0 +2             # encoder 0, two detents clockwise
12       enc 3 -1             # one detent anticlockwise

## MIDI output

fwtest models the MIDI OUT of the FM-1's sibling, the SMK-37: the transmit
side of the UART that receives the MIDI input (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-72
to HW-74, says which registers). A real FM-1 has no MIDI OUT jack, so on
the FM-1 itself these bytes go nowhere; the SMK-37 sends them through its
3.5 mm jack.

- **What goes out.** Writing the transmit count sends that many bytes from
  RAM, read at the moment of the write; writing the data register sends
  one byte. Each byte takes 320 µs on the wire (31 250 baud, whatever the
  baud and clock registers hold). A transfer started while another is
  still going waits behind it, byte for byte.
- **When it's done.** When the last byte has gone, the transmit pending
  flag is set and, if its interrupt is enabled, the UART's interrupt
  source is raised (HW-74). With the UART off nothing is sent:
  `result.json` counts the bytes in `midi_out_bytes_dropped`.
- **The capture** (`--midi-out`). `midi-out.csv` holds every byte sent,
  in order, with the time its stop bit ended: exact, at the emulated
  clock, whether core 0 is busy or waiting. `midi-out.txt` decodes them
  by the MIDI 1.0 rules, one message a line, at the time of its last byte:
  `note-on ch 1 key 60 vel 100`, `note-off`, `poly-pressure`,
  `control-change ch C ctrl N value V`, `program-change`,
  `channel-pressure`, `pitch-bend ch C value V` (0 to 16383, 8192 at
  rest), `sysex f0 ... f7 (N bytes)`, the system common and real-time
  messages by name (`clock`, `start`, `active-sensing`, ...). Channels
  count from 1. A message sent without its status byte ends
  `(running status)`; real-time bytes inside another message come out
  where they were sent. What breaks the rules is named: `stray-data XX`
  (a data byte with no status), `sysex-unterminated ...`, `incomplete
  ...` (cut short by a status byte, or at the end).
- **Golden files.** Both can be golden files, compared byte for byte (the
  times are exact, so no tolerance is needed; `rel-percent` would also let
  a byte written in decimal digits differ, so don't use it here).

## Outcomes and exit codes

| Exit | Outcome | When |
|------|---------|------|
| 0 | completed | Ran for `--ms`, and every golden file matched. (Also a halt with `--halt-ok`.) |
| 0 | power-cut | Ran to `--power-cut`, and every golden file matched. `detail` names the erase or program the cut interrupted, if any, and how many of its bytes were done. |
| 1 | golden mismatch | A golden file differs (beyond its tolerance), or an output it names is missing. |
| 2 | usage error | Bad arguments, an unreadable or oversized image, a bad script, `--out` not empty, a capture outside RAM. Nothing ran. |
| 3 | fault | A core met an instruction it cannot decode or the emulator does not implement, or its program counter left every memory that can hold code (the image, RAM, the other RAM banks), or it ran or read the code window while the flash chip was busy ("The flash chip"). |
| 4 | halt | Core 0 executed a jump to itself with interrupts disabled: a deliberate stop. The run ends there. |
| 5 | hang | The `--watchdog` word did not change for longer than its time. |

When several apply, the first in this order wins: 2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 0. Captures
and `result.json` are written for 1, 3, 4 and 5 too. Any other exit code
means fwtest itself failed.

## Instructions

fwtest runs the code the pinned toolchain's compiler emits for the
firmware's flags (`-target pi32v2 -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1`, tools/build.sh);
the two gaps the checks below found run since 0.4.0. That was checked on a corpus, not proven for
every instruction (SR-7). The corpus: the firmware at `18d9459`, the
vendored Plaits and the demo's C++ built with the firmware's CPU flags,
and several hundred small C functions written to vary types, operations
and pointer patterns, each at `-Os` and `-O2`. Two checks ran in fwtest
0.3.0, each unit on its own:

- every distinct disassembled unit of the corpus's objects (13 981; a
  dual-issue pair is one unit; some are constants in the code, decoded
  as if they were instructions);
- every form in the compiler's assembly output (660, registers and numbers
  abstracted), with each register slot set in turn to r0 to r15 (register
  pairs to each even-odd pair) and each number to values from 0 and ±1 up
  to the 32-bit limits, as far as the assembler accepts them: 34 437
  distinct encodings.

They show only that fwtest decodes and runs each one, not that it
computes what the chip does. An instruction neither check held can still
end a run as a fault ("Outcomes and exit codes"): report it as SR-7 was,
with its bytes and the smallest image that shows it.

No known gaps since fwtest 0.6.0 (0.5.0 and earlier: the pairs below,
"Both halves writing one register"). In 0.3.0 and earlier two forms ended the run as
a fault, "an instruction the emulated CPU cannot decode"; 0.4.0 runs them,
and one more change makes dual-issue pairs behave as the compiler expects:

- **Rotate by a register.** `rD = rS <> rT` (bytes `cc e1`, then two
  bytes naming the registers; `cc f1` as a pair's head), for every
  register. It rotates right by rT: the compiler emits
  `(x << s) | (x >> (32 - s))` as `rT = 32 - rT` then this, and
  `(x >> 7) | (x << 25)` as the rotate by a constant `rD = rS <> 7`. By
  0 it leaves the value (the compiler's masked rotate relies on that). An
  amount of 32 or more is taken mod 32, which the compiler's code doesn't
  show (it masks such amounts itself): don't rely on it.
- **A 4-byte push or pop of any register list.** `[--sp] = {list}` (bytes
  `d8 e8`, then the 16-bit mask, bit k for rk) and `{list} = [sp++]`
  (`d4 e8`, then the mask), without `rets` or `pc`: every list, for
  example `[--sp] = {r5-r1}`, `{r11-r6} = [sp++]` or `{r15} = [sp++]`, as
  the lists from r0 already ran. A push moves sp down by 4 a register and
  the lowest register takes the lowest address; a pop reads them back the
  same way. The compiler emits only lists from r0 (in interrupt
  handlers); lists above r0 behave the same by analogy, not checked
  against the chip.
- **Dual-issue pairs** (`A #` then `B`, as the toolchain's disassembler
  prints them): the pair's second half sees the registers as they were
  before the head, and the head's result is there after the pair. The
  compiler relies on this (in our firmware, a pair whose second half
  stores a byte back through the base register the head changes). In
  0.3.0 and earlier some 4-byte ALU forms as a pair's head wrote their result at
  once, so the second half saw the new value: which ones depended on the
  operation and the registers (of one of each family with the same
  registers, two: `r6 = r5 ^ (1 << r3) #` and `r6 = r5 >>> r3 #`).

None of the three changed any output of the firmware's suite at `cdfd067`.

**Both halves writing one register (0.6.0).** When both halves of a
dual-issue pair write the same register, the head's result is the one
there after the pair, as the compiler's code expects: it pairs a head
computing a value with a load into the same register whose result it
doesn't use, then uses the head's value (seen in flash routines:
`rA = rB + 0x80000 #` then `rA = [rC+8]`, an unused read of SPI0's
`BUF`, then `rA` as the address). fwtest 0.5.0 kept the second half's
value, so such code computed the wrong address or value there. A head
whose result equals the register's old value can't be told from one that
didn't write it; then the second half's value stays. The firmware's suite
at `6ba587e` gives the same outputs with and without the change.

### Block moves with a register base

Since 0.3.0 fwtest runs all eight modes of this 4-byte instruction (bytes
`xm eb`, then a 16-bit register mask; HARDWARE-SPEC.md HW-66). As the
toolchain's disassembler writes them, with n registers in the list:

| First byte | Form | Words moved | The base after |
|------------|------|-------------|----------------|
| `0x0N` | `{list} = [rN+]` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x1N` | `{list} = [rN++]` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | rN + 4n |
| `0x2N` | `[rN+] = {list}` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x3N` | `[rN++] = {list}` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | rN + 4n |
| `0x4N` | `{list} = [-rN]` | rN - 4n to rN - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x5N` | `{list} = [--rN]` | rN - 4n to rN - 4 | rN - 4n |
| `0x6N` | `[-rN] = {list}` | rN - 4n to rN - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x7N` | `[--rN] = {list}` | rN - 4n to rN - 4 | rN - 4n |

- The lowest-numbered register in the list takes the lowest address.
- Every address comes from the base as it was before the instruction. A
  base that is also in a loaded list, in a mode without `++` / `--`, ends
  with its loaded word (the compiler relies on this); in a write-back mode
  it ends with the written-back address. A store writes the base's
  value from before the instruction.
- An empty list moves nothing (and a write-back mode leaves the base as
  it was).
- The compiler emits the modes without `++` / `--` (`0x0`, `0x2`, `0x4`,
  `0x6`). The write-back modes, a write-back mode whose base is in its
  list, and an empty list are not established for the chip (Q-19): avoid
  relying on them.

Before 0.3.0 the four modes below the base (`0x4` to `0x7`) ended the run
as a fault, "an instruction the emulator does not implement".

## Golden files

`--golden DIR`: every file in DIR is a golden file, compared with the output
of the same name. A golden file without such an output is a mismatch. Outputs
without a golden file are not compared.

- **Exact by default:** byte for byte. Every fwtest output is deterministic,
  so exact is right unless the firmware's own behaviour is meant to vary.
- **Tolerances**, where an output is meant to be approximate: a text file
  `NAME.tolerance` beside the golden file, one line:
  - `pixel-diff N` (a `.png`): same size; each colour channel of each pixel
    within N.
  - `sample-diff N` (a `.wav`): same format and length; each sample within N.
  - `rel-percent P` (a `.csv`): same lines and fields; text fields equal;
    each integer within P percent of the golden value (at least 1). For
    example `ipb.csv` with `rel-percent 3` is the performance gate R-PERF-2
    will use.
- Golden PNG and WAV files compared with a tolerance must be ones fwtest
  wrote. To make a golden file, run once, check the output by hand, and copy
  it into the golden folder in the same commit as the test.

published container image pinned by digest in `config/fwtest-image`

```

- Run it from the repository root. The current folder is mounted read-only,
  so every input path (image, script, flash file, golden folder, suite) must
  be inside it. `--out` is created and mounted writable on its own, and must
  be empty or not exist yet.
- The container has no network and runs as your user.
- After a run, `tools/fwtest` adds `runner.txt` to the output folder, naming

## The flash chip

Since 0.6.0 fwtest's flash chip behaves as the P25Q80H's datasheet says
(`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-77, HW-78, HW-83), at its maximum times:

- **Busy times.** A page program keeps the chip busy for 3 ms and an
  erase (a 256-byte page, 4 KiB, 32 KiB, 64 KiB or the whole chip) for
  12 ms, from the moment chip select goes high. Meanwhile status register
  1 reads bit 0 (busy) and bit 1 (write enable) set, and the chip ignores
  every command but the status reads, the array and ID reads too.
- **Command rules.** An erase or program needs the write enable command
  first, or it is ignored. A program wraps within its 256-byte page and
  only clears bits.
- **The code window while busy.** While the chip is busy, a core that is
  about to run code in the code window (the image, or the chip past it),
  or reads it, ends the run as a fault: "ran code in the code window
  while the flash chip was busy (an erase or program in progress)", or
  "read the code window at ADDR while ...". That includes an interrupt
  handler in the window, and core 1. So the code that erases or
  programs, and waits, runs in RAM; so does any handler that can run
  meanwhile, with everything it calls and reads; or interrupts stay
  masked. fwtest checks only while the chip is busy: on the chip the
  window is unavailable for the whole time the firmware works the flash
  directly (HW-79), from its first command. Core 1 is checked on core
  0's clock, which it trails by at most one run call (1024 instructions).
  The audio output plays on through a busy time: it reads RAM.
- **Persistence.** The chip lasts from one run to the next only through
  files: `--flash FILE` starts a run from a saved chip (the image is
  written at `0x4000` again), `--flash-out` saves it at the end, whatever
  the outcome. Give one run's `flash.bin` to the next as `--flash`.
- **A power cut.** `--power-cut MS` ends the run at MS (in place of
  `--ms`) as if the power went then, and saves `flash.bin`. An erase or
  program in progress keeps only the part done by then: its first bytes,
  in address order, in proportion to the time gone (a 4 KiB erase cut a
  quarter of the way through has its first 1 KiB erased and the rest as
  before). That is fwtest's choice: on the chip an interrupted erase or
  program leaves those bytes undefined, so a firmware must be able to
  tell an interrupted write from a finished one (a check sum, or a marker
  written last). `--flash-log` lists every erase and program with its
  times, to aim a cut. A run that ends any other way (`--ms`, a halt, a
  fault) during an erase or program saves `flash.bin` (with
  `--flash-out`) as if that operation had finished: the bytes change when
  it starts. Use `--power-cut` for a cut.

## The command line

```
fwtest run IMAGE --ms MS --out DIR [options]
fwtest run PACKAGE --package --ms MS --out DIR [options]
fwtest suite FILE --out DIR
fwtest version
```

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--package` | The input is an update package, not a raw image ("Packages"). |
| `--ms MS` | Run for MS emulated milliseconds (up to three decimals). Required, unless `--power-cut` is given. |
| `--power-cut MS` | Run for MS emulated milliseconds, then end as a power cut: the flash keeps only the part done of an erase or program in progress, and `flash.bin` is saved ("The flash chip"). In place of `--ms`. |
| `--out DIR` | Write the outputs here. Required; must be empty or new. |
| `--script FILE` | Timed inputs (below). |
| `--flash FILE` | The flash chip's first bytes (at most 1 MiB); the rest is erased. |
| `--ram ADDR:LEN@WHEN` | Save LEN bytes of memory at ADDR at WHEN. Numbers in decimal, or hex with `0x`. Only RAM (main RAM and the other RAM banks `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` lists) can be saved; anything else is a usage error. Repeatable. |
| `--lcd WHEN` | Save the screen as a PNG at WHEN. Repeatable. |
| `--leds-every MS` | Sample the LEDs every MS into `leds.csv`. |
| `--flash-out` | Save the whole flash chip at the end (`flash.bin`). |
| `--flash-log` | Save every erase and program the chip started (`flash-ops.csv`). |
| `--wav` | Save the audio output (`audio.wav`). |
| `--ipb` | Save instructions per audio block (`ipb.csv`). |
| `--console` | Save the bytes written to the chip's debug message register (`console.txt`; `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` names it). |
| `--midi-out` | Save the MIDI output: the bytes with their times (`midi-out.csv`) and the messages they make (`midi-out.txt`). See "MIDI output". |
| `--watchdog ADDR:MS` | A hang if the 32-bit word at RAM address ADDR stays the same for more than MS ms. |
| `--halt-ok` | A halt counts as success (exit 0). |
| `--golden DIR` | Compare the outputs with the golden files in DIR (below). |

WHEN is a time in ms (`10`, `2.5`) or `end`. The run ends at `--ms`, or
earlier on a fault, halt or hang; `end` captures are taken then.

  takes bytes only by DMA into a ring, so a byte that arrives without one
  is dropped and raises nothing. The bytes' pace doesn't depend on the
  baud rate, the UART clock or the pins, which fwtest ignores.
- `midi_out_bytes_dropped`: bytes the image wrote to the MIDI output
  while its UART was off (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-74); they were not sent.
- `unmodelled_accesses`: addresses the image read or wrote that fwtest does
  not model (reads give 0, writes are dropped), with counts, up to 256.
  Usually a sign the image touched something unexpected; if the hardware
  has something there, ask for it in a spec request.

## MIDI output

fwtest models the MIDI OUT of the FM-1's sibling, the SMK-37: the transmit
side of the UART that receives the MIDI input (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-72
to HW-74, says which registers). A real FM-1 has no MIDI OUT jack, so on
the FM-1 itself these bytes go nowhere; the SMK-37 sends them through its
3.5 mm jack.

- **What goes out.** Writing the transmit count sends that many bytes from
  RAM, read at the moment of the write; writing the data register sends
  one byte. Each byte takes 320 µs on the wire (31 250 baud, whatever the
  baud and clock registers hold). A transfer started while another is
  still going waits behind it, byte for byte.
- **When it's done.** When the last byte has gone, the transmit pending
  flag is set and, if its interrupt is enabled, the UART's interrupt
  source is raised (HW-74). With the UART off nothing is sent:
  `result.json` counts the bytes in `midi_out_bytes_dropped`.
- **The capture** (`--midi-out`). `midi-out.csv` holds every byte sent,
  in order, with the time its stop bit ended: exact, at the emulated
  clock, whether core 0 is busy or waiting. `midi-out.txt` decodes them
  by the MIDI 1.0 rules, one message a line, at the time of its last byte:
  `note-on ch 1 key 60 vel 100`, `note-off`, `poly-pressure`,
  `control-change ch C ctrl N value V`, `program-change`,
  `channel-pressure`, `pitch-bend ch C value V` (0 to 16383, 8192 at
  rest), `sysex f0 ... f7 (N bytes)`, the system common and real-time
  messages by name (`clock`, `start`, `active-sensing`, ...). Channels
  count from 1. A message sent without its status byte ends
  `(running status)`; real-time bytes inside another message come out
  where they were sent. What breaks the rules is named: `stray-data XX`
  (a data byte with no status), `sysex-unterminated ...`, `incomplete
  ...` (cut short by a status byte, or at the end).
- **Golden files.** Both can be golden files, compared byte for byte (the
  times are exact, so no tolerance is needed; `rel-percent` would also let
  a byte written in decimal digits differ, so don't use it here).

## Outcomes and exit codes

| Exit | Outcome | When |
|------|---------|------|
| 0 | completed | Ran for `--ms`, and every golden file matched. (Also a halt with `--halt-ok`.) |
| 0 | power-cut | Ran to `--power-cut`, and every golden file matched. `detail` names the erase or program the cut interrupted, if any, and how many of its bytes were done. |
| 1 | golden mismatch | A golden file differs (beyond its tolerance), or an output it names is missing. |
| 2 | usage error | Bad arguments, an unreadable or oversized image, a bad script, `--out` not empty, a capture outside RAM. Nothing ran. |
| 3 | fault | A core met an instruction it cannot decode or the emulator does not implement, or its program counter left every memory that can hold code (the image, RAM, the other RAM banks), or it ran or read the code window while the flash chip was busy ("The flash chip"). |
| 4 | halt | Core 0 executed a jump to itself with interrupts disabled: a deliberate stop. The run ends there. |
| 5 | hang | The `--watchdog` word did not change for longer than its time. |

When several apply, the first in this order wins: 2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 0. Captures
and `result.json` are written for 1, 3, 4 and 5 too. Any other exit code
means fwtest itself failed.

## Instructions

fwtest runs the code the pinned toolchain's compiler emits for the
firmware's flags (`-target pi32v2 -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1`, tools/build.sh);
the two gaps the checks below found run since 0.4.0. That was checked on a corpus, not proven for
every instruction (SR-7). The corpus: the firmware at `18d9459`, the
vendored Plaits and the demo's C++ built with the firmware's CPU flags,
and several hundred small C functions written to vary types, operations
and pointer patterns, each at `-Os` and `-O2`. Two checks ran in fwtest
0.3.0, each unit on its own:

- every distinct disassembled unit of the corpus's objects (13 981; a
  dual-issue pair is one unit; some are constants in the code, decoded
  as if they were instructions);
- every form in the compiler's assembly output (660, registers and numbers
  abstracted), with each register slot set in turn to r0 to r15 (register
  pairs to each even-odd pair) and each number to values from 0 and ±1 up
  to the 32-bit limits, as far as the assembler accepts them: 34 437
  distinct encodings.

They show only that fwtest decodes and runs each one, not that it
computes what the chip does. An instruction neither check held can still
end a run as a fault ("Outcomes and exit codes"): report it as SR-7 was,
with its bytes and the smallest image that shows it.

No known gaps since fwtest 0.6.0 (0.5.0 and earlier: the pairs below,
"Both halves writing one register"). In 0.3.0 and earlier two forms ended the run as
a fault, "an instruction the emulated CPU cannot decode"; 0.4.0 runs them,
and one more change makes dual-issue pairs behave as the compiler expects:

- **Rotate by a register.** `rD = rS <> rT` (bytes `cc e1`, then two
  bytes naming the registers; `cc f1` as a pair's head), for every
  register. It rotates right by rT: the compiler emits
  `(x << s) | (x >> (32 - s))` as `rT = 32 - rT` then this, and
  `(x >> 7) | (x << 25)` as the rotate by a constant `rD = rS <> 7`. By
  0 it leaves the value (the compiler's masked rotate relies on that). An
  amount of 32 or more is taken mod 32, which the compiler's code doesn't
  show (it masks such amounts itself): don't rely on it.
- **A 4-byte push or pop of any register list.** `[--sp] = {list}` (bytes
  `d8 e8`, then the 16-bit mask, bit k for rk) and `{list} = [sp++]`
  (`d4 e8`, then the mask), without `rets` or `pc`: every list, for
  example `[--sp] = {r5-r1}`, `{r11-r6} = [sp++]` or `{r15} = [sp++]`, as
  the lists from r0 already ran. A push moves sp down by 4 a register and
  the lowest register takes the lowest address; a pop reads them back the
  same way. The compiler emits only lists from r0 (in interrupt
  handlers); lists above r0 behave the same by analogy, not checked
  against the chip.
- **Dual-issue pairs** (`A #` then `B`, as the toolchain's disassembler
  prints them): the pair's second half sees the registers as they were
  before the head, and the head's result is there after the pair. The
  compiler relies on this (in our firmware, a pair whose second half
  stores a byte back through the base register the head changes). In
  0.3.0 and earlier some 4-byte ALU forms as a pair's head wrote their result at
  once, so the second half saw the new value: which ones depended on the
  operation and the registers (of one of each family with the same
  registers, two: `r6 = r5 ^ (1 << r3) #` and `r6 = r5 >>> r3 #`).

None of the three changed any output of the firmware's suite at `cdfd067`.

**Both halves writing one register (0.6.0).** When both halves of a
dual-issue pair write the same register, the head's result is the one
there after the pair, as the compiler's code expects: it pairs a head
computing a value with a load into the same register whose result it
doesn't use, then uses the head's value (seen in flash routines:
`rA = rB + 0x80000 #` then `rA = [rC+8]`, an unused read of SPI0's
`BUF`, then `rA` as the address). fwtest 0.5.0 kept the second half's
value, so such code computed the wrong address or value there. A head
whose result equals the register's old value can't be told from one that
didn't write it; then the second half's value stays. The firmware's suite
at `6ba587e` gives the same outputs with and without the change.

### Block moves with a register base

Since 0.3.0 fwtest runs all eight modes of this 4-byte instruction (bytes
`xm eb`, then a 16-bit register mask; HARDWARE-SPEC.md HW-66). As the
toolchain's disassembler writes them, with n registers in the list:

| First byte | Form | Words moved | The base after |
|------------|------|-------------|----------------|
| `0x0N` | `{list} = [rN+]` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x1N` | `{list} = [rN++]` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | rN + 4n |
| `0x2N` | `[rN+] = {list}` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x3N` | `[rN++] = {list}` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | rN + 4n |
| `0x4N` | `{list} = [-rN]` | rN - 4n to rN - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x5N` | `{list} = [--rN]` | rN - 4n to rN - 4 | rN - 4n |
| `0x6N` | `[-rN] = {list}` | rN - 4n to rN - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x7N` | `[--rN] = {list}` | rN - 4n to rN - 4 | rN - 4n |

- The lowest-numbered register in the list takes the lowest address.
- Every address comes from the base as it was before the instruction. A
  base that is also in a loaded list, in a mode without `++` / `--`, ends
  with its loaded word (the compiler relies on this); in a write-back mode
  it ends with the written-back address. A store writes the base's
  value from before the instruction.
- An empty list moves nothing (and a write-back mode leaves the base as
  it was).
- The compiler emits the modes without `++` / `--` (`0x0`, `0x2`, `0x4`,
  `0x6`). The write-back modes, a write-back mode whose base is in its
  list, and an empty list are not established for the chip (Q-19): avoid
  relying on them.

Before 0.3.0 the four modes below the base (`0x4` to `0x7`) ended the run
as a fault, "an instruction the emulator does not implement".

## Golden files

`--golden DIR`: every file in DIR is a golden file, compared with the output
of the same name. A golden file without such an output is a mismatch. Outputs
without a golden file are not compared.

- **Exact by default:** byte for byte. Every fwtest output is deterministic,
  so exact is right unless the firmware's own behaviour is meant to vary.
- **Tolerances**, where an output is meant to be approximate: a text file
  `NAME.tolerance` beside the golden file, one line:
  - `pixel-diff N` (a `.png`): same size; each colour channel of each pixel
    within N.
  - `sample-diff N` (a `.wav`): same format and length; each sample within N.
  - `rel-percent P` (a `.csv`): same lines and fields; text fields equal;
    each integer within P percent of the golden value (at least 1). For
    example `ipb.csv` with `rel-percent 3` is the performance gate R-PERF-2
    will use.
- Golden PNG and WAV files compared with a tolerance must be ones fwtest
  wrote. To make a golden file, run once, check the output by hand, and copy
  it into the golden folder in the same commit as the test.

6:# Requirements
121:| R-MIDIOUT-1 | MIDI out's sender (M6b; firmware/src/midi_out.c): a queue of messages that only the engine's block callback writes and drains, so nothing waits for the wire; the transmitter (UART1's transmit DMA, HW-73, HW-74) starts a transfer only when the last one has gone, of whole messages up to 12 bytes, and never changes a transfer's bytes while it runs. Running status: a channel message leaves out its status when it repeats the last one sent while the wire is busy; after the queue empties and the wire goes quiet the next message carries its status; system common messages end it, realtime doesn't. In fwtest, in every MIDI out case: no two bytes closer than a byte's time (320 us); every run of bytes back to back is one transfer of at most 12, as many as the firmware started; every byte the firmware handed on is on the wire, in whole messages (none broken); a message after a gap of more than two blocks carries its status. | M6b | C-FW-SUITE |
129:| R-STORE-1 | The store (M7) is our own design (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M7; docs/STORE-FORMAT.md) since M8a in the stock layout's unused region, chip offsets `0xFC000` to `0xFEFFF` (HW-80; one definition; M7 used the stock user patch region, `0xEA000` to `0xFBFFF`), clear of the boot area, the Bluetooth sector, the stock firmware's user patch region and the per-unit last sector; the image is linked to end before the user patch region, and no run of the store's tests changes the chip outside the store but for fwtest's own image (persist and wear start with the user patch region full of a pattern, which they leave unchanged). tools/store.py reads and writes the same format, and its constants are the firmware's. | M7 | C-UNIT, C-FW-SUITE |
170:| R-PKG-1 | Phase A1 (docs/A1-PLAN.md, Note A1-1): `tools/fwsc.py` packs the firmware's package link (`tools/build.sh`'s `app-pkg.bin`, the same code linked at `0x02000120`, HW-91; what runs from RAM byte for byte the raw image's) into a `.fwsc` from HARDWARE-SPEC.md HW-87 to HW-91 only: one entry, the flash image, ending at the app area's end (nothing written past it), no loader in it, the same bytes from the same input; its reader runs fwtest's checks in fwtest's order, and refuses a package broken at each of them at that check. | A1 | C-UNIT, C-PACKAGE |
171:| R-PKG-2 | The package boots in fwtest's package path (`--package`, docs/HARNESS.md "Packages") as the raw image does: in the firmware suite's main cases the same outcome, time, instructions and outputs (the r0 block the boot block, the flash chip from the stock user patch region on the same), `run.package` our identity, the app area `0x04000` and the entry `0x02000120`; and fwtest refuses each broken package with the reader's words for that check. | A1 | C-PACKAGE |
| R-PERF-5 | The gates are tested against the unmodified build, measured in the same run: a deliberately slower build fails the speed gate and the steady-state budget (and no other) when the unmodifie
| R-PLAITS-1 | The platform load test (M4b, the owner's request): Mutable Instruments' Plaits, vendored unmodified (R-REPRO-7), builds as its own demo image (`tools/build.sh build --demo plaits`, from
| R-PLAITS-2 | The demo's soft-float routines (our own) are correctly rounded IEEE 754 binary32: in fwtest, every operation the compiler calls them for gives, bit for bit, the result an exact rational
| R-PLAITS-3 | For each of Plaits' 24 engines the record gives core 0's instructions per audio block in fwtest, at its heaviest over a fixed set of settings and its mean, with soft-float and with the 
| R-PLAITS-4 | Its audio is clean: no NaN, infinity or out-of-range conversion in soft-float over the whole bench; the same sound (checksums) with hardware float as with soft-float; and a note played

/*
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
 * SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
 *
 * The engine seam (BR-1; docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, "Seams for firmwares
 * built on small-beeps"; docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md). Built with
 * SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL, main() leaves out the base's FM engine and its
 * store start-up and calls these three instead, which the firmware built
 * on the base defines. Without it main() runs the base's instrument, as
 * before, and nothing here is called.
 *
 * - sb_engine_init: once, where the base calls fm_init(): after the time
 *   base, the tick's and SPI1's handlers and the panel's scan are set up,
 *   before interrupts are on and before the audio starts. The engine
 *   starts its own parts here (MIDI in with midi_start(), core 1 with
 *   sb_core1_start(), the store with store_init(), ...). Interrupts are
 *   off: nothing it sets up runs yet.
 * - sb_engine_block: the block callback main hands to audio_start()
 *   (audio.h): run by core 0 in the audio interrupt, every block, with
 *   AUDIO_FRAMES stereo frames to fill. MIDI in (midi_poll, midi_read)
 *   and MIDI out (midi_out_send, midi_out_poll) are read and written
 *   from here, as the base's engine does.
 * - sb_engine_serve: from main's loop, once before the loop begins and
 *   then on each wake that found work (a change of sb_work, sb.h): the
 *   tick's whole seconds, the panel's events, the screen's next frame,
 *   and anything that adds one to sb_work. Long work (the store's flash
 *   writes, drawing) goes here, never in the block callback. Before it
 *   is called main has brought up the screen and shown the test screen;
 *   main keeps the heartbeat on it while sb_beacon.screen is
 *   SB_SCREEN_TEST, so an engine that draws its own sets another value.
 */

#ifndef ENGINE_H
#define ENGINE_H

#include "sb.h"

void sb_engine_init(void);
void sb_engine_block(s32 *out, u32 frames);
void sb_engine_serve(void);

#endif

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""The tests of the seams for firmwares built on small-beeps (clean-1027;
docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, "Seams for firmwares built on small-beeps";
docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md), check C-SEAMS.

  seams_suite.py --build DIR --out DIR [--only NAME ...]

DIR is build A's outputs (tools/build.sh build). Each case builds what it
needs with tools/build.sh into OUT/<case>/ and runs it in fwtest
(tools/fwtest, the pinned image) where it runs anything. The cases:

- writeback (R-BUILD-4): a test build holding a store that writes back
  into the register it stores (SB_TEST_WRITEBACK, firmware/src/probe.c)
  is refused, its message naming the object, the function and the
  instruction; build A, which passed the same check, holds none.

Prints what each case saw, and exits 1 if any failed.
"""

import argparse
import os
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))


def sh(argv, log, check=True):
    """Runs argv from the repository root, its output into log; returns
    (exit code, output)."""
    p = subprocess.run(argv, cwd=ROOT, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    out = p.stdout.decode("utf-8", "replace")
    with open(log, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("$ %s\n%s\n" % (" ".join(argv), out))
    if check and p.returncode:
        raise RuntimeError("%s failed (%d); see %s" % (argv[0], p.returncode, log))
    return p.returncode, out


def build(out, log, *opts, check=True):
    return sh(["sh", "tools/build.sh", "build", "--out", out] + list(opts), log, check)


# --- writeback ------------------------------------------------------------

def case_writeback(a, work, log):
    problems = []
    rc, out = build(os.path.join(work, "build"), log, "--define", "SB_TEST_WRITEBACK", check=False)
    if rc == 0:
        problems.append("the SB_TEST_WRITEBACK build was not refused")
    if not re.search(r"^probe\.o: sb_test_writeback\+0x[0-9a-f]+ \(\.text[^)]*\): \[\+\+r1=4\] = r1$", out, re.M):
        problems.append("the refusal does not name probe.o, sb_test_writeback and its store")
    if "FAIL: a store writes back into the register it stores" not in out:
        problems.append("no FAIL line")
    if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(a.build, "app.elf")):
        problems.append("build A has no app.elf")
    print("writeback: the test build %s; build A passed the check" % ("refused" if rc else "NOT refused"))
    return problems


CASES = [
    ("writeback", case_writeback),
]


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n")[0])
    ap.add_argument("--build", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--out", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--only", nargs="*")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    a.build = os.path.abspath(a.build)
    out = os.path.abspath(a.out)
    shutil.rmtree(out, ignore_errors=True)
    os.makedirs(out)
    failed = []
    for name, fn in CASES:
        if a.only and name not in a.only:
            continue
        work = os.path.join(out, name)
        os.makedirs(work)
        log = os.path.join(work, "log.txt")
        try:
            problems = fn(a, work, log)
        except RuntimeError as e:
            problems = [str(e)]
        for p in problems:
            print("  FAIL %s: %s" % (name, p))
        if problems:
            failed.append(name)
    print("seams suite: %s" % ("FAIL (%s)" % ", ".join(failed) if failed else "PASS"))
    return 1 if failed else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

### 2026-10-27 clean-1027: seams for firmwares built on small-beeps

small-beeps is meant to be a base other people build their own firmwares
on. A firmware built on it asked, in general terms, for seams: places
where it can add its own engine and use the platform's parts without
changing the base's files. Each seam here is general, for any such
firmware; docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md says how to use them. Each
pull request adds one, with its tests in `tools/seams_suite.py` (check
C-SEAMS) and its part below.

#### The write-back store check (R-BUILD-3)

- **What.** A store with write-back, `[++rN=k] = rN` or `[rN++=k] = rN`
  (also byte and half-word stores, k a number or a register), stores its
  own base register. Whether the chip stores the base's value from
  before the increment or after it is open (SR-10, the spec side's).
  Until it is answered no image of ours may hold one, so the build
  refuses it.
- **How.** `tools/build.sh` disassembles every object (`objdump -d`,
  which shows code sections only) before linking, and
  `tools/writeback.pl` flags each such store with the object, the
  function, the offset and the instruction. Not the linked image: its
  RAM part holds the constants after the code, which would decode as
  instructions. The matcher is unit-tested on the disassembler's own
  text (`tests/test_writeback.py`), and C-SEAMS builds a test image
  holding one (`SB_TEST_WRITEBACK`, an inline store in `probe.c`) and
  checks the build is refused.
- **Today's firmware holds none**, at #126's head and at every seam's:
  the shipping image and its package link pass the check, and so does
  every test build CI makes. The image is unchanged by the check (the
  same `app.bin`).
- **The one exception.** The Plaits demo's measurement builds with the
  hardware float instructions (`PLAITS_HWFLOAT`, M4b) hold 68 such
  stores, all in the vendored Plaits (17 objects), where the compiler
  writes them for float stores. Those builds only ever run in fwtest,
  to measure what the float instructions would save, so the check lists
  and counts them there and lets the build go on; everywhere else,
  including a firmware build that defines `PLAITS_HWFLOAT`, it refuses.
  The demo's soft-float builds hold none. Should SR-10's answer show
  the chip stores something other than fwtest does, the
  hardware-float measurements would need running again.
EOF
python3 tools/check-private.py 2>&1 | tail -1

content.content:
cmd_inside() {
    src=$1 out=$2
    cd "$src"
    # The chip's CPU model and its single-precision float instructions, as
    # the SDK builds for it (HW-62, since M5). The Plaits demo's own C is
    # built without them, as before (build_demo_plaits): its soft-float
    # test must exercise the soft-float routines, and `-mcpu=r3` on its
    # own already makes the compiler use the instructions.
    CPU="-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1"
    # -nostdinc: no C library headers either; the SDK's register headers
    # are the only outside includes. -fno-common puts zeroed data in .bss.
    CFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -Os -g
            -fno-common -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
            -Ifirmware/src -Ivendor/jieli-sdk/include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -D$d"; done
    # Assembly is built without -g, which would record the source path.
    ASFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -nostdinc -Werror"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do ASFLAGS="$ASFLAGS -D$d"; done
    # C++ from outside folders (BR-5): the C flags' CPU, warnings and
    # freestanding build, C++14 without exceptions, RTTI or guarded
    # statics.
    CXXFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -x c++ -std=c++14 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -Os -g
              -fno-common -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics -Wall -Wextra -Werror
              -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=. -Ifirmware/src"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CXXFLAGS="$CXXFLAGS -D$d"; done
    clang --version | head -1
    ld --version | head -1
    echo "SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH"
    # Objects are intermediate: kept out of the outputs.
    obj=/tmp/small-beeps-obj
    rm -rf "$obj" && mkdir -p "$obj"
    objs=""

#### Building with outside sources (BR-5, R-BUILD-4)

- **What.** `tools/build.sh build` takes `--src DIR` (repeatable): every
  `.c`, `.S` and `.cc` under a folder outside `firmware/` is built into
  the image; and `--leave-out FILE` (repeatable): a base source, named
  by its path from the repository's root, is left out, so a firmware can
  replace a base file or do without it. With `--define` (already there
  for test builds) that is all a firmware built on the base needs to be
  built with the base's own build image, its files kept in its own
  repository and the base's used unmodified.
- **The same flags.** C with the firmware's flags; assembly with the
  firmware's (and, new, the `--define`s, which a firmware's `.S` may
  test); C++ as C++14 with the same CPU, warnings-as-errors and
  freestanding flags, without exceptions, RTTI or guarded statics (the
  toolchain's clang 4.0.1 knows no C++17). Each source gets `-I` for its
  own folder; the base's headers are on the path as for the firmware.
- **Names.** Base objects are named by their file name, as before (the
  default image is unchanged: the same `app.bin`). An outside object is
  named by its path, `src<N>_<path>.o`, so a file named as a base file
  is (`probe.c`, say) is built beside the base's, never over it; two
  definitions of one function then fail the link, as they should.
- **Deterministic.** Each folder is mounted read-only beside the source
  mount, as `sb-src-N`, and built by its path from the source mount
  (`../sb-src-1/...`), as the base's files are built by theirs. Clang
  4.0.1 keeps an absolute source path in the objects even with
  `-fdebug-prefix-map`; a relative one it keeps as given. So where the
  folder sits on the host, and where the source is mounted (C-BUILD-B),
  never reaches an output: C-SEAMS builds the same folder from three
  places, once with the source mounted elsewhere, and gets the same
  bytes; the build's own check that no output holds the source path now
  covers each outside mount too.
- **Refused:** a folder holding the base (its sources would be built
  twice), one inside `firmware/` (built already), a path with a space,
  and a `--leave-out` that names no base source (a typo would otherwise
  build the base file silently).
- **From another repository.** The firmware built on the base keeps the
  base as a folder (a git submodule or a clone) and runs the base's
  script from there: `sh base/tools/build.sh build --out out --src src
  --define ...`. The script builds the base's pinned build image the
  first time (`tools/build.sh image`) and runs everything inside it, so
  the firmware gets the same toolchain and the same deterministic build
  (docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md).

content.text: Writing BR-1's test engine as an outside folder (it uses BR-5): an engine that counts its init, blocks and serves, plays a quiet square wave and counts key presses.

lines: + * SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
+ * SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
+ * A test engine on the engine seam (firmware/src/engine.h, BR-1), built
+ * from outside firmware/ (tools/build.sh --src tests/seams/engine
+ * --define SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL) by tools/seams_suite.py, case engine. It
+ * counts what main asks of it in a record the suite reads by its ELF
+ * symbol, plays a quiet square wave, and counts the panel's key presses.
+#include "audio.h"
+#include "engine.h"
+#include "input.h"
+#define TEST_ENGINE_MARKER 0x31474E45u   /* "ENG1" in memory order */
+#define HALF_PERIOD        50u           /* frames: about 441 Hz */
+#define LEVEL              (AUDIO_FULL / 16)
+struct sb_test_engine_record {
+    u32 marker;
+    u32 inits;          /* sb_engine_init calls */
+    u32 init_ticks;     /* the tick's interrupts taken before it: 0, as interrupts are off */
+    u32 init_blocks;    /* audio blocks before it: 0, as the audio starts after */
+    u32 blocks;         /* sb_engine_block calls */
+    u32 frames;         /* frames they were asked for */
+    u32 serves;         /* sb_engine_serve calls */
+    u32 serve_seconds;  /* sb_seconds at the last */
+    u32 presses;        /* key presses the block callback took */
+    u32 serve_presses;  /* presses seen by the last serve */
+volatile struct sb_test_engine_record sb_test_engine;
+static u32 phase;
+void sb_engine_init(void)
+    sb_test_engine.marker = TEST_ENGINE_MARKER;
+    sb_test_engine.inits++;
+    sb_test_engine.init_ticks = sb_beacon.tick_count;
+    sb_test_engine.init_blocks = sb_audio.blocks;
+void sb_engine_block(s32 *out, u32 frames)
+    struct input_event e;
+    while (input_read_audio(&e))
+        if (e.kind == INPUT_PRESS)
+            sb_test_engine.presses++;
+    for (n = 0; n < frames; n++) {
+        s32 s = phase < HALF_PERIOD ? LEVEL : -LEVEL;
+        out[2 * n] = s;
+        phase = (phase + 1) % (2 * HALF_PERIOD);
+    sb_test_engine.blocks++;
+    sb_test_engine.frames += frames;
+void sb_engine_serve(void)
+    sb_test_engine.serves++;
+    sb_test_engine.serve_seconds = sb_seconds;
+    sb_test_engine.serve_presses = sb_test_engine.presses;

  base's FM engine and its store start-up (`fm_init()`, `store_boot()`)

#### The platform without the instrument (BR-2, R-PLAT-1)

- **The platform's files:** boot (`crt0.S`, `start.c`), interrupts
  (`irq.c`), the tick, the loop and the beacon (`main.c`), input
  (`input.c`), audio (`audio.c`), the LCD and screen (`lcd.c`, `gfx.c`,
  `font.c`, `screen.c`), MIDI in and out (`midi.c`, `midi_out.c`), the
  store (`store.c`), and the test builds' `probe.c`. **The instrument's:**
  `fm.c`, `fm_play.c`, `patches.c`, `arp.c`, `views.c`, `saving.c`,
  `spectrum.c`, and for now `core1.S`, whose entry calls the FM engine's
  core-1 loop (BR-3 makes core 1's start the platform's). `tools/build.sh`
  lists them once (`INSTRUMENT`). Only `main.c` called the instrument,
  and since BR-1 it doesn't when built with `SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL`; the
  test builds' references are inside their own defines.
- **`tools/build.sh build --platform`** leaves the instrument's files
  out, defines `SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL` and links with
  `firmware/platform.ld`; the engine comes from `--src` (BR-5). With
  `--ld SCRIPT` an engine links with a script of its own (in the base or
  in a `--src` folder) that includes the platform's (`INCLUDE
  platform.ld`; the build passes `-L firmware`) and asserts its own
  records; the package link uses the same script.
- **The linker scripts.** `firmware/platform.ld` is what `app.ld` was,
  less the instrument: the memory, the sections, the stacks and the
  assertions about the platform's records. `firmware/app.ld` includes it
  and asserts the instrument's records. The image is unchanged
  (`da13d093…`); only the ELF's section names differ.
- **Where an engine's records go.** The records sit at fixed addresses
  that the tests (and the app) read, and the FM engine's record sits
  between the audio record and MIDI's. A platform-only link would slide
  MIDI's, MIDI out's and the store's records down by its size. So the
  64 bytes there are now the **engine's slot** (`.beacon.engine0`,
  `0x01C00590`): kept whether anything fills them or not (the script
  moves the location counter past them), at most 64 bytes (more and the
  link fails, as the counter would have to move back), the FM engine's
  record in the base. After the store's record come the **engine's
  records** (`.beacon.engine1` to `.beacon.engine4` in that order, then
  `.beacon.engine`, from `0x01C00870`), as large as they need: the
  base's interface record and arpeggiator's take the first two, so they
  stay at `0x01C00870` and `0x01C008D0`; a firmware on the platform alone
  gets `0x01C00870` for its first.
- **Tested** (C-SEAMS, case platform): the test engine linked with the
  platform alone and its own script (which asserts its record at
  `0x01C00870`). The ELF holds none of the instrument's functions or
  records, the platform's records are where the base has them, the
  package link is built too, and the engine case's whole run passes on
  it. The platform alone is 11 180 bytes of code (the firmware: 52 840).
EOF

cat >> docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md <<'EOF'

#### Core 1's start, the platform's (BR-3, R-CORE1-1)

- **What.** Starting core 1 and handing it work were the FM engine's
  (M5, "Two cores"): `core1.S`'s entry called the engine's loop on a
  stack of its own, `fm_init()` pointed source 126's vector word at it
  and set C1_CON bit 3 (HW-9), and `fm_play.c` kept the lock and the
  shared loads (HW-65). The Plaits bench had its own copy of the entry
  and the start. Now the platform has one of each (`core1.h`):
  - `sb_core1_start(entry, stack_top)`: core 0 leaves the entry and the
    stack's top where the entry (`core1_entry.S`) finds them, points the
    vector word at it, sets the bit, and waits (`SB_CORE1_WAIT` polls,
    about 1 ms in fwtest) for core 1 to say it runs; then puts the word
    back and returns 1, or 0 if core 1 never said so. On core 1, the
    entry sets both stack pointers from the given top and calls
    `sb_core1_main` (`core1.c`), which says it runs, under the lock, and
    calls the engine's entry; if that returns, core 1 stops with
    interrupts off.
  - `sb_lock`, `sb_unlock`, `sb_shared`, `sb_publish`: the lock byte
    taken by test-and-set with csync around, a shared word read after
    csync, a shared word written under a lock. `static inline`, as they
    are short and sit in core 0's per-block path (the FM engine posts a
    block and waits for its answer with them).
- **The FM engine** keeps its own stack (1 KiB, as before, now a
  `static` array in `fm_play.c`), its job's lock and sequence numbers,
  and its loop; it starts core 1 with `sb_core1_start(fm_core1_main,
  ...)` and keeps its two-core fallback (the result). Core 1's flag that
  it runs is the platform's now, so `fm_core1_main` only sets
  `sb_fm.core1`. **The Plaits bench** starts its core 1 the same way, on
  its own 8 KiB stack, and its copy of the entry is gone.
- **A name clash on the way.** The base names its objects by file name,
  so `core1.c` and `core1.S` both made `core1.o` and the link failed
  ("multiple definition"); the entry is `core1_entry.S`.
- **The image changes** (code 53 028 bytes, from 52 960); the firmware's
  suites pass as they are (below, in the pull request).
- **Tested** (C-SEAMS, cases engine and platform): the test engine
  starts core 1 and hands it a job every block, a sequence number to
  triple: core 1 starts, does exactly one job a block, every answer
  right and in time, and the vector word holds its stub again, with the
  instrument linked and with the platform alone.
EOF

/*
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
 * SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
 *
 * Single-precision floating point in software, for the Plaits demo
 * (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M4b). The compiler turns every float operation
 * into a call to one of these when there is no floating-point unit; we
 * don't link the toolchain's own (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md), so these are ours,
 * written from IEEE 754's definition of binary32:
 *
 * - add, subtract, multiply, divide and square root are correctly rounded
 *   to nearest, ties to even, with subnormals, signed zeros, infinities
 *   and NaN (any NaN result is the quiet NaN 0x7FC00000);
 * - comparisons follow the usual soft-float return conventions, so that a
 *   NaN makes every ordered comparison false;
 * - float to integer truncates toward zero and saturates out of range (NaN
 *   gives 0), so a wild value never turns into an arbitrary one;
 * - invalid operations, overflows and bad conversions are counted in
 *   softfloat_flags, IEEE's exception flags as counts, so the bench can
 *   show Plaits made no NaN and no infinity.
 *
 * Only integer operations are used inside (a float operator here would
 * call itself), and no 64-bit shift or division, which would need more
 * helpers: products are split into 32-bit halves by hand. The image test
 * PLAITS_TEST_SOFTFLOAT checks every routine bit for bit against a
 * reference (tools/plaits-bench.py).
 */

#include "sb.h"

#### SysEx bytes from MIDI in (BR-7, R-MIDI-8)

- **What.** MIDI in's parser skipped System Exclusive, counting it (M6a).
  A firmware built on the base may need its bytes (a dump of its own
  data, for one, of a few kilobytes). `midi_sysex_tap(fn)` sets a
  function the parser calls with each SysEx byte and what it is:
  `MIDI_SYSEX_BEGIN` (the F0), `MIDI_SYSEX_DATA` (each data byte),
  `MIDI_SYSEX_END` (the F7) or `MIDI_SYSEX_CUT` (any other status byte
  that ends it: a new F0, a channel or system common status, or a
  reset; the byte then also does what it always does). Realtime bytes
  inside a SysEx (a clock, say) never reach the tap: they are messages
  of their own, handed on by `midi_read()`, and the SysEx goes on after
  them, as MIDI 1.0 has it. The parser is otherwise unchanged: its
  counts, and `MIDI_SYSEX_LIMIT`, which only counts a message long, so a
  message of any length reaches the tap whole.
- **A tap, not pieces through `midi_read()`.** `midi_read()` hands on
  whole messages of at most two data bytes, and the instrument and the
  arpeggiator read it once a block; giving it SysEx in pieces would
  change what every reader sees. A tap changes nothing for a firmware
  that sets none (the base sets none), and costs one test of a pointer
  per SysEx byte.
- **Where it runs, and where the work goes.** The tap runs where the
  parser runs: in `midi_read()`, from the engine's block callback, core
  0's audio interrupt. So it should only keep the bytes (into a buffer
  of the firmware's) and, at the end, add one to `sb_work` to wake
  main; the work on them (checking, decoding, storing) goes in main's
  loop, `sb_engine_serve()` (BR-1). At the wire's pace a block brings at
  most five bytes, so the tap's share of a block is small whatever the
  message's length; a 4 104-byte message takes 1.3 s to arrive.
- **The image changes** (code 53 068 bytes, from 53 028): the pointer
  tests in the parser.
- **Tested** (C-SEAMS, case sysex) on the test engine linked with the
  platform alone, which starts MIDI in and keeps each message's bytes

  bytes, with a clock byte in its middle, arrives whole and in order

#### SysEx bytes from MIDI in (BR-7, R-MIDI-8)

- **What.** MIDI in's parser skipped System Exclusive, counting it (M6a).
  A firmware built on the base may need its bytes (a dump of its own
  data, for one, of a few kilobytes). `midi_sysex_tap(fn)` sets a
  function the parser calls with each SysEx byte and what it is:
  `MIDI_SYSEX_BEGIN` (the F0), `MIDI_SYSEX_DATA` (each data byte),
  `MIDI_SYSEX_END` (the F7) or `MIDI_SYSEX_CUT` (any other status byte
  that ends it: a new F0, a channel or system common status, or a
  reset; the byte then also does what it always does). Realtime bytes
  inside a SysEx (a clock, say) never reach the tap: they are messages
  of their own, handed on by `midi_read()`, and the SysEx goes on after
  them, as MIDI 1.0 has it. The parser is otherwise unchanged: its
  counts, and `MIDI_SYSEX_LIMIT`, which only counts a message long, so a
  message of any length reaches the tap whole.
- **A tap, not pieces through `midi_read()`.** `midi_read()` hands on
  whole messages of at most two data bytes, and the instrument and the
  arpeggiator read it once a block; giving it SysEx in pieces would
  change what every reader sees. A tap changes nothing for a firmware
  that sets none (the base sets none), and costs one test of a pointer
  per SysEx byte.
- **Where it runs, and where the work goes.** The tap runs where the
  parser runs: in `midi_read()`, from the engine's block callback, core
  0's audio interrupt. So it should only keep the bytes (into a buffer
  of the firmware's) and, at the end, add one to `sb_work` to wake
  main; the work on them (checking, decoding, storing) goes in main's
  loop, `sb_engine_serve()` (BR-1). At the wire's pace a block brings at
  most five bytes, so the tap's share of a block is small whatever the
  message's length; a 4 104-byte message takes 1.3 s to arrive.
- **The image changes** (code 53 068 bytes, from 53 028): the pointer
  tests in the parser.
- **Tested** (C-SEAMS, case sysex) on the test engine linked with the
  platform alone, which starts MIDI in and keeps each message's bytes
  through the tap and sums them in its serve: a message of 4 104 data
  bytes, with a clock byte in its middle, arrives whole and in order
  (length, a sum weighted by place, first and last byte), the work done
  in the serve; the clock is handed on as a message; a second message
  cut short by a note on is reported cut by 0x90, and the note handed
  on; MIDI's record counts the first long and drops nothing. The
  firmware's own MIDI cases (C-FW-SUITE) check MIDI in is as before.
EOF
