mk core1 <<'EOF'
**Seventh in the merge order, after #161. Cumulative: it carries everything before it; its own commits are the last two.**

**What:** BR-3, core 1's start as a platform function (`firmware/src/core1.h`, `core1.c`, `core1_entry.S`).
- `sb_core1_start(entry, stack_top)` releases core 1 into an entry on a given stack. It returns 1 once core 1 runs, or 0 if it never says so, and puts back the vector word it borrows (HW-9).
- `sb_lock`, `sb_unlock`, `sb_shared` and `sb_publish` (HW-65) moved out of `fm_play.c` with neutral names. They are `static inline`, as they were.
- The FM engine and the Plaits bench use them. The bench's own core-1 entry is gone, and `fm_play.c` keeps its own 1 KiB stack.
- The test engine starts core 1 and hands it a job every block. Adds **R-CORE1-1** and the DESIGN-NOTES part.

**Why:** clean-1027, section 2, BR-3.

**How:** `core1.S` became `core1_entry.S`, because base objects are named by file name and `core1.c` and `core1.S` both made `core1.o`.

**One golden changed by hand** (its own commit, as the timing goldens' policy asks for a change that is not a pure time shift):
- The image starts 2 to 3 µs later. In midiout's MIDI capture, the chord's three keys, pressed in the same instant, now reach the engine as 60, 64, 67 (was 64, 67, 60). Which key the scan sees first depends on its phase against the script.
- Every other message is identical, only 2 to 3 µs later. The case's own checks accept the chord in any order.
- midiround's script is rewritten from the new capture.
- The order is the same on every later seam's image.

**Result** (local, fwtest 0.8.0, image `203f527f…`, code 53 028 bytes):
- firmware suite: see the comment below once its rerun finishes. Its first run was cut off by the host (SIGTERM); its only failure was this golden.
- ARP suite **PASS**, package suite **PASS**, presets **70 of 70**, release selftest **PASS**, Plaits bench **PASS**.
- C-SEAMS **PASS**. With the instrument linked and with the platform alone, core 1 starts, does exactly one job a block, gets every answer right and in time, and its vector word is restored.

EOF
mk runtime <<'EOF'
**Eighth in the merge order, after the BR-3 PR. Cumulative; its own commit is the last one.**

**What:** BR-4, the C++ runtime and `mem*` in the platform (`firmware/runtime/`).
- Moved from the Plaits demo:
  - `memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset`, `__cxa_pure_virtual`, `operator delete` and the soft-float routines;
  - the freestanding headers (`<algorithm>`, `<cmath>`, `<math.h>`, `<stddef.h>`, `<inttypes.h>`), now in `firmware/runtime/include/`.
- New:
  - `<string.h>`;
  - `__cxa_atexit` and `__dso_handle`: a static object with a destructor failed the link without them;
  - `.ctors`, placed by `platform.ld` and run by `main()` before an engine's init (`SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL` only). A static object with a constructor used to fail the link as an orphan section.
- The runtime is an archive that the link takes last, so an image gets only the members it calls. Without `--gc-sections`, a plain object would add code to the firmware.
- Also: the test engine runs C++ that needs all of the above, **R-RT-1**, and the DESIGN-NOTES part.

**Why:** clean-1027, section 2, BR-4.

**Result:**
- The firmware's `app.bin` is unchanged (BR-3's `203f527f…`), and build A holds none of the runtime (C-SEAMS checks this).
- The test engine's C++ gives the expected 1301: a virtual class, `std::sort`, `mem*` with run-time lengths, and a constructed static object. That holds both with the instrument linked and with the platform alone.
- All four demo builds link.
- Note for the audit: vendored Plaits is base code only for files under `firmware/demos/plaits/` (`audit/audit.json`). The moved runtime files don't resemble Plaits, so this changes nothing material.

EOF
mk sysex <<'EOF'
**Ninth in the merge order, after the BR-4 PR. Cumulative; its own commit is the last one.**

**What:** BR-7, SysEx bytes from MIDI in. `midi_sysex_tap(fn)` sets a function that MIDI in's parser calls for every byte of a System Exclusive message, in order and however long the message is:
- begin (F0), each data byte, then end (F7) or cut (the status byte that ends it);
- realtime bytes inside never reach the tap, and the message goes on after them.

The tap runs where `midi_read()` runs (the block callback), so it keeps the bytes and wakes main; the work goes in `sb_engine_serve` (BR-1). The test engine does exactly that. Also: C-SEAMS case `sysex`, **R-MIDI-8**, and the DESIGN-NOTES part.

**Why:** clean-1027, section 2, BR-7. I used a tap rather than SysEx in pieces through `midi_read()`, which would change what every reader of it sees.

**Result:**
- Code 53 068 bytes (from 53 028).
- In fwtest, on the platform alone: a message of 4 104 data bytes with a clock byte in the middle reaches the tap whole and in order, and the work runs in the serve. The clock is handed on as a message, a second message cut short by a note on is reported cut by 0x90, and no byte is dropped.
- C-SEAMS **PASS**. The `midiout` capture keeps BR-3's order on this image.

EOF
mk midiout <<'EOF'
**Tenth in the merge order, after the BR-7 PR. Cumulative; its own commit is the last one.**

**What:** BR-8, raw bytes to MIDI out.
- `midi_out_raw(buf, len)` streams a buffer through the transmitter as it is: a transfer of up to 12 bytes whenever the wire is free.
- Queued messages wait until the stream has gone, except realtime ones, which go out between its transfers (MIDI 1.0 allows them inside SysEx). The next message carries its status.
- `midi_out_raw_busy()` says when the buffer is free again.
- Counts go in `sb_midi_out_raw`, found by symbol: MIDI out's record ends where the store's begins, so it can't grow.
- Also: C-SEAMS case `rawout`, **R-MIDIOUT-9**, and the DESIGN-NOTES part.

**Why:** clean-1027, section 2, BR-8.

**How:** the stream is handed over through a sequence number that the poll answers, so main's loop (where SysEx work goes) may call it. The queue's policy holds meanwhile. The first version of the test queued a note every 8th block, so about 23 notes waited behind the 250 ms stream and the policy dropped 13 messages, which is the designed behaviour. The test now queues one every 16th block; the policy itself is covered by the `midiburst` case.

**Result:**
- Code 53 340 bytes.
- On the wire: the test engine's 600-byte SysEx arrives in order, with only clocks inside it (about 200). Every note follows the F7, the first one with its status. Every clock and note is sent.
- C-SEAMS **PASS**.

EOF
mk store <<'EOF'
**Eleventh in the merge order, after the BR-8 PR. Cumulative; its own commit is the last one.**

**What:** BR-9, storage for large records.
- Kinds 0x80 to 0xFE are kept for firmwares built on the base, with any id. A reset voids them with everything else.
- `store_put`/`store_get` take a payload of up to 5 904 bytes for these kinds:
  - written as parts of up to 492 bytes (a 512-byte record);
  - the index and count go in the header's two bytes that were always 0;
  - a tag (the write's own number) is the payload's first word;
  - a payload is read whole or not at all.
- `tools/store.py` models it. Also: STORE-FORMAT.md ("Kinds for firmwares built on the base"), unit tests, C-SEAMS case `store`, **R-STORE-10**, and the DESIGN-NOTES part.

**Why:** clean-1027, section 2, BR-9. A record can't leave its 4 KiB sector, so a 4 096-byte payload has to span records.

**How much today's region holds (three sectors, unchanged), from the model:**
- **Alone:** a payload of up to **5 396 bytes**, rewritten as often as asked. A 4 096-byte payload leaves 1.3 KB to spare.
- **Beside the base's full store** (16 user slots, the selection and the settings, saved in between): it depends on how the records fall in the sectors. **2 952 bytes** held in all 40 histories of 300 rewrites; **4 096 not reliably**.
- Past what fits, a write is refused (`STORE_ERR_FULL`) and what was there stays.
- **Not atomic.** Keeping the old payload through a whole rewrite needs two copies (8 192 bytes), and the ring has about 8 160. So a write cut short leaves the old payload until the new write's first part is whole, then nothing until its last part is. It is never a mix; the model checks every cut point.
- Where a larger region goes is your later decision.

**Result:**
- Code 54 416 bytes, RAM +1 312 bytes.
- In fwtest, nine runs chained through the flash file:
  - a 4 096-byte payload is written, read at the next start-up, then rewritten;
  - another rewrite is cut part way by a power cut: the payload is gone afterwards and the small payload beside it stays;
  - rewritten after the cut, then a reset voids both;
  - alone, 5 000 bytes are written and read back, and 5 904 are refused.
- The model reads what the firmware does after every run.
- C-SEAMS **PASS**, unit tests **PASS**. The base's own store cases: see the firmware suite run on the chain's head (comment below).

EOF
mk guide <<'EOF'
**Twelfth and last in the merge order, after the BR-9 PR. Cumulative; its own commits are the last ones.**

**What:**
- `docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md`, a plain guide for someone making their own firmware on the base. It covers:

**Why:** clean-1027, section 2: the guide.

**How:** every command and example in the guide was run as written:

- the image boots in fwtest;
- it packs into a `.fwsc` that the reader passes, and boots from the package.

**Result:** as above. The low-profile check **PASS**.

set -eu

INSTRUMENT="firmware/src/arp.c firmware/src/fm.c firmware/src/fm_play.c
            firmware/src/patches.c firmware/src/saving.c firmware/src/spectrum.c firmware/src/views.c"

ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
PLATFORM=linux/amd64

sha256() {
    if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then sha256sum "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1
    else shasum -a 256 "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1; fi
}

image_tag() {
    echo "small-beeps-build:$(sha256 "$ROOT/tools/Dockerfile" | cut -c1-16)"
}

cmd_image() {

    docker build --platform "$PLATFORM" -t "$(image_tag)" - < "$ROOT/tools/Dockerfile"
    docker image inspect --format 'image {{.Id}}' "$(image_tag)"

cmd_build() {
    out="" src_mount=/mnt/small-beeps-src defines="" demo="" mounts="" srcs="" leave="" n=0
    platform="" ldscript=""
    while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
        case "$1" in
            --out) out=$2; shift 2 ;;
            --platform) platform=1; shift ;;
            --ld)

                ldscript="$(cd "$(dirname "$2")" && pwd)/$(basename "$2")"; shift 2 ;;
            --src)

                    "$d"/*) echo "build: --src $2 holds the base itself; give the folders of your own sources" >&2; exit 2 ;;

                case "$d/" in
                    "$ROOT/firmware/"*) echo "build: --src $2 is inside firmware/, which is built already" >&2; exit 2 ;;

                n=$((n + 1))
                srcs="$srcs $d"
                shift 2 ;;
            --leave-out)
                case "$2" in
                    firmware/*) [ -f "$ROOT/$2" ] || { echo "build: --leave-out $2: no such base file" >&2; exit 2; } ;;
                    *) echo "build: --leave-out takes a base source's path from the repository's root (firmware/...)" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                leave="$leave $2"; shift 2 ;;
            --src-mount) src_mount=$2; shift 2 ;;
            --define)
                case "$2" in
                    ''|*[!A-Z0-9_]*) echo "build: --define takes a NAME of A-Z, 0-9 and _" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                defines="$defines $2"; shift 2 ;;
            --demo)
                case "$2" in
                    plaits) demo=$2 ;;
                    *) echo "build: --demo takes plaits" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                shift 2 ;;
            *) echo "unknown option $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    [ -n "$out" ] || { echo "build: --out DIR is required" >&2; exit 2; }
    if [ -n "$platform" ]; then
        [ -z "$demo" ] || { echo "build: --platform and --demo don't go together" >&2; exit 2; }
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        leave="$leave $(echo $INSTRUMENT)"
        defines="$defines SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL"

    # or from the outside folder (sb-src-N) that holds it.
    script=firmware/app.ld
    [ -z "$platform" ] || script=firmware/platform.ld

        case "$ldscript" in
            "$ROOT"/*) script=${ldscript#"$ROOT"/} ;;
        esac

# The image's size in bytes, from the symbols firmware/app.ld defines:
# code (code and constants, in the image, wherever they run), data
# (initialised data: in the image and copied to RAM), bss (zeroed RAM, the
# beacon included), image (the raw image's length), stack (reserved at the
# top of RAM, both stacks), irq_stack (the lower part of it: the interrupt
# stack) and, since M7, ram_code (the part of code copied to RAM and run
# there, which takes RAM as data does).
write_size() {
    sym() { nm "$1" | awk -v s="$2" '$3 == s { print $1 }'; }
    hex() { printf '%d' "0x$1"; }
    origin=$(hex 02000000)
    data_load=$(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_load)")
    data=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_start)") ))
    bss=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __bss_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __bss_start)") ))
    stack=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_top)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_limit)") ))
    irq=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __irq_stack_top)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_limit)") ))
    ram_code=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __ram_code_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __ram_code_start)") ))
    printf 'code %d\ndata %d\nbss %d\nimage %d\nstack %d\nirq_stack %d\nram_code %d\n' \
        $((data_load - origin + ram_code)) $((data - ram_code)) "$bss" $((data_load - origin + data)) \
        "$stack" "$irq" "$ram_code"
}

# The Plaits demo's own sources and the vendored Plaits (M4b,
# docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md): our C glue and runtime with the firmware's flags;
# our C++ with the same warnings, as errors (Plaits' headers are system
# headers to it: their warnings are not ours to fix); the vendored files
# unmodified at upstream's -O2, with warnings off. All the C++ is built in
# upstream's portable configuration (-DTEST), with our standard headers
# and plaits_pre.h in place of a C library's. Objects are named after their
# paths, since vendored names repeat.
build_demo_plaits() {
    d=firmware/demos/plaits
    CXX="clang -target pi32v2 -x c++ -std=c++11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -fno-exceptions
         -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics -fno-common -g -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
         -I$d/include -Ifirmware/runtime/include -isystem vendor/plaits/eurorack -isystem vendor/plaits
         -I$d -Ifirmware/src
         -DTEST -include $d/include/plaits_pre.h"
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CXX="$CXX -D$d2"; done
    # PLAITS_HWFLOAT: the toolchain's hardware single-precision float
    # instructions (its fprev1 feature) instead of our soft-float, for the
    # C++ only: a measurement of what they would save, never the demo's
    # default, since whether the chip has them is open (SR-5).
    case " ${SB_DEFINES:-} " in
        *" PLAITS_HWFLOAT "*) CXX="$CXX -Xclang -target-feature -Xclang +fprev1" ;;
    esac
    defs=""
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do defs="$defs -D$d2"; done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS $defs -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2046
            *) set -x; clang $(echo "$CFLAGS" | sed 's/ -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1//') -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        set -x; $CXX -Os -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        $CXX -O2 -w -c "$s" -o "$o"
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    echo "built $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | wc -l) vendored Plaits files"
}

# The sources of the folders given with --src (BR-5), mounted beside the
# source mount as sb-src-N: every .c, .S and .cc, sorted by path, named
# by it, and built by its path from the source mount.
build_outside() {
    k=0
    for m in ${SB_SRCS:-}; do
        k=$((k + 1))
        r=../sb-src-$k
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        for s in $(cd "$m" && find . -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' -o -name '*.cc' | sed 's|^\./||' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
            o="$obj/src${k}_$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/; s/\.cc$/.o/')"
            case "$s" in
                *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS -I"$r" -c "$r/$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
                *.cc) set -x; clang $CXXFLAGS -I"$r" -c "$r/$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
                *) set -x; clang $CFLAGS -Ifirmware/runtime/include -I"$r" -c "$r/$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            esac
            objs="$objs $o"
        done
    done
}

# The platform's runtime (firmware/runtime/, BR-4): memcpy, memmove and
# memset, what C++ needs (cxx.cc) and soft-float, in an archive the link
# takes last, so an image gets only the members it calls (the firmware:
# none). Its C is built without the float instructions, as soft-float's
# must be (and as the Plaits demo's C always was).
build_runtime() {
    rt=""
    for s in $(find firmware/runtime -name '*.c' -o -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/runtime_$(basename "$s" | sed 's/\.c$/.o/; s/\.cc$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *.cc) set -x; clang $CXXFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2046
            *) set -x; clang $(echo "$CFLAGS" | sed 's/ -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1//') -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        rt="$rt $o"
    done
    rm -f "$obj/libsb_runtime.a"
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    ar rcD "$obj/libsb_runtime.a" $rt
}

cmd_inside() {
    src=$1 out=$2
    cd "$src"
    # The chip's CPU model and its single-precision float instructions, as
    # the SDK builds for it (HW-62, since M5). The Plaits demo's own C is
    # built without them, as before (build_demo_plaits): its soft-float
    # test must exercise the soft-float routines, and `-mcpu=r3` on its
    # own already makes the compiler use the instructions.
    CPU="-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1"
    # -nostdinc: no C library headers either; the SDK's register headers
    # are the only outside includes. -fno-common puts zeroed data in .bss.
    CFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -Os -g
            -fno-common -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
            -Ifirmware/src -Ivendor/jieli-sdk/include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -D$d"; done
    # Assembly is built without -g, which would record the source path.
    ASFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -nostdinc -Werror"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do ASFLAGS="$ASFLAGS -D$d"; done
    # C++ from outside folders (BR-5): the C flags' CPU, warnings and
    # freestanding build, C++14 without exceptions, RTTI or guarded
    # statics.
    CXXFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -x c++ -std=c++14 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -Os -g
              -fno-common -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics -Wall -Wextra -Werror
              -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=. -Ifirmware/src -Ifirmware/runtime/include"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CXXFLAGS="$CXXFLAGS -D$d"; done
    clang --version | head -1
    ld --version | head -1
    echo "SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH"
    # Objects are intermediate: kept out of the outputs.
    obj=/tmp/small-beeps-obj
    rm -rf "$obj" && mkdir -p "$obj"
    objs=""
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        # The demo is an engine on the engine seam (firmware/src/engine.h).
        CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -DSB_DEMO_PLAITS -DSB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL -Ifirmware/demos/plaits"
    fi
    for s in $(find firmware/src -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        case " ${SB_LEAVE_OUT:-} " in
            *" $s "*) echo "left out: $s"; continue ;;
        esac
        o="$obj/$(basename "$s" | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *) set -x; clang $CFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        build_demo_plaits
    fi
    build_outside
    build_runtime

    # clean-1027; tools/ownbase.pl, R-BUILD-3): every object's code is
    # checked before anything is linked, so no image holds one. One
    # exception: the Plaits demo's measurement builds with the hardware
    # float instructions (PLAITS_HWFLOAT, which only fwtest ever runs),
    # where the compiler puts such stores in the vendored Plaits; there
    # they are listed and counted, not refused.
    wb=0
    for o in $objs $rt; do
        objdump -d "$o" | perl tools/ownbase.pl "$(basename "$o")" || wb=$((wb + 1))
    done
    if [ "$wb" -ne 0 ]; then
        case " ${SB_DEMO:-}:${SB_DEFINES:-} " in
            *plaits:*" PLAITS_HWFLOAT "*)
                echo "ownbase check: $wb objects with such stores (above), allowed in a PLAITS_HWFLOAT measurement build" ;;

                exit 1 ;;
        esac

    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    ld -nostdlib --no-undefined --orphan-handling=error -L firmware -T "${SB_LD:-firmware/app.ld}" \
        -o "$out/app.elf" $objs "$obj/libsb_runtime.a"

    # right after it. This objcopy takes one section at a time, and ld's
    # own binary output gets data addresses wrong, so the two are joined.
    objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/app.elf" "$obj/text.bin"
    objcopy -O binary -j .data "$out/app.elf" "$obj/data.bin"
    cat "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin" > "$out/app.bin"
    # The package link (Phase A1, HW-91): the same objects, linked where a
    # package's app.bin runs, 0x120 past the window's start; its raw image
    # is what tools/fwsc.py packs into a .fwsc. Not for a demo.
    if [ -z "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        ld -nostdlib --no-undefined --orphan-handling=error --defsym=IMAGE_ORIGIN=0x02000120 \
            -L firmware -T "${SB_LD:-firmware/app.ld}" -o "$out/app-pkg.elf" $objs "$obj/libsb_runtime.a"
        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/app-pkg.elf" "$obj/pkg-text.bin"
        objcopy -O binary -j .data "$out/app-pkg.elf" "$obj/pkg-data.bin"
        cat "$obj/pkg-text.bin" "$obj/pkg-data.bin" > "$out/app-pkg.bin"
    fi
    set +x
    write_size "$out/app.elf" > "$out/app.size"
    cat "$out/app.size"
    image=$(awk '$1 == "image" { print $2 }' "$out/app.size")
    if [ "$(wc -c < "$out/app.bin")" -ne "$image" ]; then
        echo "FAIL: app.bin is not the $image bytes app.ld lays out" >&2; exit 1
    fi
    # Nothing in the firmware may depend on which link it is (A1-1): what
    # runs from RAM is byte for byte the same in both, the boot code (run
    # from the window) is as long, and the package's starts at 0x02000120.
    # The RAM check is the firmware's, not a test build's: the store's wipe
    # test (SB_TEST_STORE_WIPE) turns a link symbol into a chip offset.
    if [ -z "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        [ -n "${SB_DEFINES:-}" ] || cmp "$obj/data.bin" "$obj/pkg-data.bin" \
            || { echo "FAIL: the package link's RAM code and data differ from the raw image's" >&2; exit 1; }
        [ "$(wc -c < "$obj/pkg-text.bin")" -eq "$(wc -c < "$obj/text.bin")" ] \
            || { echo "FAIL: the package link's boot code is not as long as the raw image's" >&2; exit 1; }
        [ "$(nm "$out/app-pkg.elf" | awk '$3 == "_start" { print $1 }')" = 02000120 ] \
            || { echo "FAIL: the package link's _start is not at 0x02000120" >&2; exit 1; }
        rm "$obj/pkg-text.bin" "$obj/pkg-data.bin"
    fi
    rm "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin"
    # No output may contain the absolute source path, or an outside
    # folder's mount path.
    for f in $(find "$out" -type f | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        for p in "$src" ${SB_SRCS:-}; do
            if grep -q -F "$p" "$f"; then
                echo "FAIL: $f contains the source path $p" >&2; exit 1
            fi
        done
    done
    (cd "$out" && find . -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS | sed 's|^\./||' \
        | LC_ALL=C sort | xargs sha256sum > SHA256SUMS)
}

case "${1:-}" in
    image) cmd_image ;;
    image-tag) image_tag ;;
    build) shift; cmd_build "$@" ;;
    inside) shift; cmd_inside "$@" ;;
    *) sed -n '5,12p' "$0" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

# The image's size in bytes, from the symbols firmware/app.ld defines:
# code (code and constants, in the image, wherever they run), data
# (initialised data: in the image and copied to RAM), bss (zeroed RAM, the
# beacon included), image (the raw image's length), stack (reserved at the
# top of RAM, both stacks), irq_stack (the lower part of it: the interrupt
# stack) and, since M7, ram_code (the part of code copied to RAM and run
# there, which takes RAM as data does).
write_size() {
    sym() { nm "$1" | awk -v s="$2" '$3 == s { print $1 }'; }
    hex() { printf '%d' "0x$1"; }
    origin=$(hex 02000000)
    data_load=$(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_load)")
    data=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_start)") ))
    bss=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __bss_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __bss_start)") ))
    stack=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_top)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_limit)") ))
    irq=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __irq_stack_top)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_limit)") ))
    ram_code=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __ram_code_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __ram_code_start)") ))
    printf 'code %d\ndata %d\nbss %d\nimage %d\nstack %d\nirq_stack %d\nram_code %d\n' \
        $((data_load - origin + ram_code)) $((data - ram_code)) "$bss" $((data_load - origin + data)) \
        "$stack" "$irq" "$ram_code"
}

# The Plaits demo's own sources and the vendored Plaits (M4b,
# docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md): our C glue and runtime with the firmware's flags;
# our C++ with the same warnings, as errors (Plaits' headers are system
# headers to it: their warnings are not ours to fix); the vendored files
# unmodified at upstream's -O2, with warnings off. All the C++ is built in
# upstream's portable configuration (-DTEST), with our standard headers
# and plaits_pre.h in place of a C library's. Objects are named after their
# paths, since vendored names repeat.
build_demo_plaits() {
    d=firmware/demos/plaits
    CXX="clang -target pi32v2 -x c++ -std=c++11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -fno-exceptions
         -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics -fno-common -g -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
         -I$d/include -Ifirmware/runtime/include -isystem vendor/plaits/eurorack -isystem vendor/plaits
         -I$d -Ifirmware/src
         -DTEST -include $d/include/plaits_pre.h"
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CXX="$CXX -D$d2"; done
    # PLAITS_HWFLOAT: the toolchain's hardware single-precision float
    # instructions (its fprev1 feature) instead of our soft-float, for the
    # C++ only: a measurement of what they would save, never the demo's
    # default, since whether the chip has them is open (SR-5).
    case " ${SB_DEFINES:-} " in
        *" PLAITS_HWFLOAT "*) CXX="$CXX -Xclang -target-feature -Xclang +fprev1" ;;
    esac
    defs=""
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do defs="$defs -D$d2"; done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS $defs -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2046
            *) set -x; clang $(echo "$CFLAGS" | sed 's/ -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1//') -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        set -x; $CXX -Os -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        $CXX -O2 -w -c "$s" -o "$o"
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    echo "built $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | wc -l) vendored Plaits files"
}

# The sources of the folders given with --src (BR-5), mounted beside the
# source mount as sb-src-N: every .c, .S and .cc, sorted by path, named
# by it, and built by its path from the source mount.
build_outside() {
    k=0
    for m in ${SB_SRCS:-}; do
        k=$((k + 1))
        r=../sb-src-$k
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        for s in $(cd "$m" && find . -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' -o -name '*.cc' | sed 's|^\./||' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
            o="$obj/src${k}_$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/; s/\.cc$/.o/')"
            case "$s" in
                *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS -I"$r" -c "$r/$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
                *.cc) set -x; clang $CXXFLAGS -I"$r" -c "$r/$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
                *) set -x; clang $CFLAGS -Ifirmware/runtime/include -I"$r" -c "$r/$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            esac
            objs="$objs $o"
        done
    done
}

# The platform's runtime (firmware/runtime/, BR-4): memcpy, memmove and
# memset, what C++ needs (cxx.cc) and soft-float, in an archive the link
# takes last, so an image gets only the members it calls (the firmware:
# none). Its C is built without the float instructions, as soft-float's
# must be (and as the Plaits demo's C always was).
build_runtime() {
    rt=""
    for s in $(find firmware/runtime -name '*.c' -o -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/runtime_$(basename "$s" | sed 's/\.c$/.o/; s/\.cc$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *.cc) set -x; clang $CXXFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2046
            *) set -x; clang $(echo "$CFLAGS" | sed 's/ -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1//') -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        rt="$rt $o"
    done
    rm -f "$obj/libsb_runtime.a"
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    ar rcD "$obj/libsb_runtime.a" $rt
}

cmd_inside() {
    src=$1 out=$2
    cd "$src"
    # The chip's CPU model and its single-precision float instructions, as
    # the SDK builds for it (HW-62, since M5). The Plaits demo's own C is
    # built without them, as before (build_demo_plaits): its soft-float
    # test must exercise the soft-float routines, and `-mcpu=r3` on its
    # own already makes the compiler use the instructions.
    CPU="-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1"
    # -nostdinc: no C library headers either; the SDK's register headers
    # are the only outside includes. -fno-common puts zeroed data in .bss.
    CFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -Os -g
            -fno-common -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
            -Ifirmware/src -Ivendor/jieli-sdk/include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -D$d"; done
    # Assembly is built without -g, which would record the source path.
    ASFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -nostdinc -Werror"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do ASFLAGS="$ASFLAGS -D$d"; done
    # C++ from outside folders (BR-5): the C flags' CPU, warnings and
    # freestanding build, C++14 without exceptions, RTTI or guarded
    # statics.
    CXXFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -x c++ -std=c++14 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -Os -g
              -fno-common -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics -Wall -Wextra -Werror
              -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=. -Ifirmware/src -Ifirmware/runtime/include"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CXXFLAGS="$CXXFLAGS -D$d"; done
    clang --version | head -1
    ld --version | head -1
    echo "SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH"
    # Objects are intermediate: kept out of the outputs.
    obj=/tmp/small-beeps-obj
    rm -rf "$obj" && mkdir -p "$obj"
    objs=""
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        # The demo is an engine on the engine seam (firmware/src/engine.h).
        CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -DSB_DEMO_PLAITS -DSB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL -Ifirmware/demos/plaits"
    fi
    for s in $(find firmware/src -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        case " ${SB_LEAVE_OUT:-} " in
            *" $s "*) echo "left out: $s"; continue ;;
        esac
        o="$obj/$(basename "$s" | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *) set -x; clang $CFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        build_demo_plaits
    fi
    build_outside
    build_runtime
    # No store that writes back into the register it stores (since
    # clean-1027; tools/ownbase.pl, R-BUILD-3): every object's code is
    # checked before anything is linked, so no image holds one. One
    # exception: the Plaits demo's measurement builds with the hardware
    # float instructions (PLAITS_HWFLOAT, which only fwtest ever runs),
    # where the compiler puts such stores in the vendored Plaits; there
    # they are listed and counted, not refused.
    wb=0
    for o in $objs $rt; do
        objdump -d "$o" | perl tools/ownbase.pl "$(basename "$o")" || wb=$((wb + 1))
    done
    if [ "$wb" -ne 0 ]; then
        case " ${SB_DEMO:-}:${SB_DEFINES:-} " in
            *plaits:*" PLAITS_HWFLOAT "*)
                echo "ownbase check: $wb objects with such stores (above), allowed in a PLAITS_HWFLOAT measurement build" ;;
            *)
                echo "FAIL: a store writes back into the register it stores (above; tools/ownbase.pl)" >&2
                exit 1 ;;
        esac
    fi
    set -x
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    ld -nostdlib --no-undefined --orphan-handling=error -L firmware -T "${SB_LD:-firmware/app.ld}" \
        -o "$out/app.elf" $objs "$obj/libsb_runtime.a"
    # The raw image is the code, then the initial data, which app.ld loads
    # right after it. This objcopy takes one section at a time, and ld's
    # own binary output gets data addresses wrong, so the two are joined.
    objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/app.elf" "$obj/text.bin"
    objcopy -O binary -j .data "$out/app.elf" "$obj/data.bin"
    cat "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin" > "$out/app.bin"
    # The package link (Phase A1, HW-91): the same objects, linked where a
    # package's app.bin runs, 0x120 past the window's start; its raw image
    # is what tools/fwsc.py packs into a .fwsc. Not for a demo.
    if [ -z "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        ld -nostdlib --no-undefined --orphan-handling=error --defsym=IMAGE_ORIGIN=0x02000120 \
            -L firmware -T "${SB_LD:-firmware/app.ld}" -o "$out/app-pkg.elf" $objs "$obj/libsb_runtime.a"
        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/app-pkg.elf" "$obj/pkg-text.bin"
        objcopy -O binary -j .data "$out/app-pkg.elf" "$obj/pkg-data.bin"
        cat "$obj/pkg-text.bin" "$obj/pkg-data.bin" > "$out/app-pkg.bin"
    fi
    set +x
    write_size "$out/app.elf" > "$out/app.size"
    cat "$out/app.size"
    image=$(awk '$1 == "image" { print $2 }' "$out/app.size")
    if [ "$(wc -c < "$out/app.bin")" -ne "$image" ]; then
        echo "FAIL: app.bin is not the $image bytes app.ld lays out" >&2; exit 1
    fi
    # Nothing in the firmware may depend on which link it is (A1-1): what
    # runs from RAM is byte for byte the same in both, the boot code (run
    # from the window) is as long, and the package's starts at 0x02000120.
    # The RAM check is the firmware's, not a test build's: the store's wipe
    # test (SB_TEST_STORE_WIPE) turns a link symbol into a chip offset.
    if [ -z "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        [ -n "${SB_DEFINES:-}" ] || cmp "$obj/data.bin" "$obj/pkg-data.bin" \
            || { echo "FAIL: the package link's RAM code and data differ from the raw image's" >&2; exit 1; }
        [ "$(wc -c < "$obj/pkg-text.bin")" -eq "$(wc -c < "$obj/text.bin")" ] \
            || { echo "FAIL: the package link's boot code is not as long as the raw image's" >&2; exit 1; }
        [ "$(nm "$out/app-pkg.elf" | awk '$3 == "_start" { print $1 }')" = 02000120 ] \
            || { echo "FAIL: the package link's _start is not at 0x02000120" >&2; exit 1; }
        rm "$obj/pkg-text.bin" "$obj/pkg-data.bin"
    fi
    rm "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin"
    # No output may contain the absolute source path, or an outside
    # folder's mount path.
    for f in $(find "$out" -type f | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        for p in "$src" ${SB_SRCS:-}; do
            if grep -q -F "$p" "$f"; then
                echo "FAIL: $f contains the source path $p" >&2; exit 1
            fi
        done
    done
    (cd "$out" && find . -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS | sed 's|^\./||' \
        | LC_ALL=C sort | xargs sha256sum > SHA256SUMS)
}

case "${1:-}" in
    image) cmd_image ;;
    image-tag) image_tag ;;
    build) shift; cmd_build "$@" ;;
    inside) shift; cmd_inside "$@" ;;
    *) sed -n '5,12p' "$0" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
'

lines: Embedded audio experiments. Work in progress.
MIT licensed (see `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`). How changes are made and recorded:
-`CONTRIBUTING.md`. What is planned: `docs/PLAN.md`. Building your own on
-this base: `docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md`.
+`CONTRIBUTING.md`. What is planned: `docs/PLAN.md`.
## Build
-SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
-SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
-# Building your own firmware on small-beeps
-small-beeps is a base: a platform that starts the chip and runs the
-panel, the screen, the audio output, MIDI in and out and the flash store,
-plus an FM instrument that uses it. You can keep the platform as it is and
-put your own engine where the instrument was, in your own repository,
-without changing a file of the base. This guide shows how, from an empty
-repository to a firmware running in fwtest and in the F-Emulator app.
-Everything here is MIT-licensed, like the rest of small-beeps: keep its
-`LICENSE` and `NOTICE` with your copy. The seams this guide uses are
-described in more depth in docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, "Seams for firmwares
-built on small-beeps", and their requirements are in docs/REQUIREMENTS.md
-(R-ENG-1, R-PLAT-1, R-CORE1-1, R-RT-1, R-MIDI-8, R-MIDIOUT-9, R-STORE-10,
-R-BUILD-3, R-BUILD-4).
-## 1. Set up
-You need git, Docker (any host; the build and the tests run as
-linux/amd64 containers) and Python 3.9 or later.
-mkdir my-firmware && cd my-firmware && git init
-git submodule add https://github.com/japes98/small-beeps base
-mkdir src
-sh base/tools/build.sh image      # once: the pinned build image, made locally
-`build.sh image` builds the base's build image on your machine: a pinned
-Debian with the chip's toolchain, downloaded from its vendor and checked
-against its SHA-256 (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md). The image and the toolchain are
-never published anywhere; keep them out of your repository too.
-Your repository then holds `base/` (the base, unmodified, at a commit you
-choose) and `src/` (your sources). Everything below runs from your
-repository's root.
-## 2. Write your engine
-Your engine is three functions (`base/firmware/src/engine.h`):
-#include "audio.h"
-#include "engine.h"
-#include "input.h"
-#include "midi.h"
-#include "midi_out.h"
-void sb_engine_init(void)
-    midi_settings_default(&midi_settings);   /* MIDI's settings: out on channel 1, ... */
-    midi_start();                            /* the UART, for MIDI in and out */
-void sb_engine_block(s32 *out, u32 frames)
-    struct input_event e;
-    struct midi_msg m;
-    while (input_read_audio(&e))
-        ;                                    /* the panel's events: keys, encoders, the pot */
-    midi_poll();
-    while (midi_read(&m))
-        ;                                    /* MIDI in's messages */
-    for (n = 0; n < frames; n++)
-        out[2 * n] = out[2 * n + 1] = 0;     /* your sound: 24-bit, left then right */
-    midi_out_poll();                         /* send what you queued */
-void sb_engine_serve(void)
-    /* slow work: the screen, the store, a SysEx you received */
-| Function | When | Where it runs |
-| `sb_engine_init` | once, at start-up, before interrupts are on and the audio starts | core 0, main |
-| `sb_engine_block` | every audio block: `AUDIO_FRAMES` (64) stereo frames, 1.45 ms | core 0, the audio interrupt |
-| `sb_engine_serve` | once before main's loop, then whenever something added work | core 0, main's loop |
-- **The block callback must keep up**: a block is 1.45 ms of core 0's
-  time, shared with the tick and the panel's scan. Do the sound and the
-  quick reactions here, nothing that waits.
-- **Waking main.** Main sleeps between interrupts and calls your serve
-  when `sb_work` (`sb.h`) changed: the tick adds one each whole second,
-  the panel's scan one per event. Add one yourself (`sb_work++`) from the
-  block callback when you leave main work, as a finished SysEx message.
-- **The screen.** Main brings the screen up and shows a test screen with
-  a heartbeat. To draw your own, set `sb_beacon.screen` to another value
-  (`SB_SCREEN_PANEL`, `sb.h`), so main stops drawing the heartbeat, then
-  draw into the frame buffer with `gfx_*` and send rows with
-  `lcd_send_rows()` or a rectangle with `lcd_send_rect()` (`sb.h`; wait
-  for `lcd_busy()` to be 0 first), from your serve.
-- **C++** works too: name the file `.cc`. The platform's runtime has
-  `memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset`, `<algorithm>`, `<string.h>`,
-  `<inttypes.h>`, `<stddef.h>`, `<math.h>` and what virtual classes and
-  static objects need (`base/firmware/runtime/`); there is no heap, no
-  exceptions and no RTTI. Static objects' constructors run before your
-  init.
-## 3. What the platform gives you
-All from `base/firmware/src/`, all yours to call:
-| Part | Header | What |
-| The panel | `input.h` | events (`input_read_audio` in the block callback, `input_read` in main), each control's value (`input_value`), the LEDs (`input_led`) |
-| Audio | `audio.h` | the block size and rate; your block callback fills the buffer |
-| The screen | `sb.h` | `gfx_fill`, `gfx_text`, `gfx_line`, ...; `lcd_send_rows`, `lcd_send_rect`, `lcd_busy` |
-| MIDI in | `midi.h` | `midi_start`, `midi_poll` and `midi_read` (whole messages, from the block callback); `midi_sysex_tap` (System Exclusive's bytes, below) |
-| MIDI out | `midi_out.h` | below, section 7 |
-| The store | `store.h` | `store_init` (once, in your init), `store_get`, `store_put`, `store_reset`, below |
-| Core 1 | `core1.h` | `sb_core1_start(entry, stack_top)`; `sb_lock`, `sb_unlock`, `sb_shared`, `sb_publish` to hand it work |
-| Time | `sb.h` | `sb_now()` (24 MHz), `sb_ticks()`, `sb_wait_ms()` (main only), the heartbeat in `sb_beacon` |
-**System Exclusive in.** `midi_sysex_tap(fn)` sets a function MIDI in's
-parser calls for each byte of a System Exclusive message:
-`MIDI_SYSEX_BEGIN`, each `MIDI_SYSEX_DATA` byte, then `MIDI_SYSEX_END` or
-`MIDI_SYSEX_CUT`. It runs in the block callback: keep the bytes in a
-buffer of your own and, at the end, add one to `sb_work`; work on them in
-your serve. Messages of any length come through (tested with 4 104 data
-bytes).
-**The store.** Kinds `0x80` to `0xFE` are yours, any id from 0 to 255,
-and a payload of up to 5 904 bytes each (`STORE_FW_MAX`):
-store_init();                                     /* in your init */
-n = store_get(0x80, 0, buf, sizeof buf, &version);  /* -1: none */
-r = store_put(0x80, 0, 1, buf, len);              /* from your serve: it waits for the flash */
-A payload is read whole or not at all: if the power goes during a write,
-the old one is still there until the new write's first part is written,
-and then there is none until you write it again. Write from your serve,
-never from the block callback (a write takes the flash for some
-milliseconds). The store's region today is three sectors (12 KiB): with
-nothing else in it, it holds and rewrites one payload of up to 5 396
-bytes; `store_put` returns `STORE_ERR_FULL` past what fits, and what was
-there stays. `store_reset()` voids everything (a factory reset).
-docs/STORE-FORMAT.md has the bytes.
-## 4. Your records in RAM
-Tests read state at fixed RAM addresses. The platform keeps its records
-at the start of RAM (`base/firmware/platform.ld`) and keeps two places
-for an engine's:
-- the engine's slot, `0x01C00590`: one record of at most 64 bytes, in
-  section `.beacon.engine0`;
-- after the store's record, from `0x01C00870`: sections
-  `.beacon.engine1` to `.beacon.engine4`, then `.beacon.engine`, in that
-  order, any size.
-volatile struct my_record my_record __attribute__((section(".beacon.engine1")));
-Write a linker script of your own that includes the platform's and
-asserts where your records landed, so a change shows at link time:
-/* src/my.ld */
-INCLUDE platform.ld
-ASSERT(my_record == 0x01C00870, "my record must follow the store's")
-## 5. Build
-sh base/tools/build.sh build --out out --platform --src src --ld src/my.ld
-| Option | What |
-| `--platform` | leaves out the base's instrument (its FM engine, presets, arpeggiator, screens and saving), builds with `SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL`, links with `platform.ld` |

-The outputs, in `out/`:
-- `app.bin`: the raw image (linked at `0x02000000`), what fwtest and the
-  app run;
-- `app-pkg.bin`: the same code linked at `0x02000120`, for a `.fwsc`

-## 6. Test with fwtest, run in the app
-**fwtest** runs your image in an emulator of the chip, from its pinned
-container image: keys, encoders, the pot and MIDI in from a script; the
-screen, the audio, MIDI out, RAM and the flash chip out.
-sh base/tools/fwtest run out/app.bin --ms 3000 --out out/t1 \
-    --script tests/keys.txt --wav --midi-out --lcd 2500 \
-Paths must be inside the folder you run it from (your repository's
-root). docs/HARNESS.md (`base/docs/HARNESS.md`) is its manual: the script
-format, every output, the flash chip's timing and power cuts
-(`--flash`, `--flash-out`, `--power-cut`), golden files and suites. The
-base's own tests of these seams are a working example:
-`base/tools/seams_suite.py` with its test engine in
-`base/tests/seams/engine/`.
-**The F-Emulator app** runs the same image:
-- the bare image: open `out/app.bin` in the app;
-- or a package: pack the package link into a `.fwsc` and check it with
-  the reader fwtest also uses:
-  python3 base/tools/fwsc.py pack out/app-pkg.bin --version 0.1.0 \
-      --identity my-firmware-0.1.0 --out out/my-firmware.fwsc
-  python3 base/tools/fwsc.py out/my-firmware.fwsc
-  sh base/tools/fwtest run out/my-firmware.fwsc --package --ms 2000 --out out/t2
-  The identity is at most 19 characters and must not begin with another
-  board's name (`fwsc.py` says which).
-## 7. MIDI out
-**What the base sends for you:** nothing, once you build with
-`--platform`. The base's instrument sends the panel's notes, knobs and
-program changes, passes MIDI thru and sends the arpeggiator's clock; all
-of that is the instrument's, and goes with it. The platform only sends
-what your engine queues.
-**Sending your own:**
-- Call `midi_start()` in your init (it turns the UART on for both
-  directions) and `midi_settings_default(&midi_settings)` (the out
-  channel, 1, comes from there).
-- From the block callback, queue messages with `midi_out_channel(kind,
-  d1, d2)` (on the out channel) or `midi_out_send(&msg)` (any status),
-  and call `midi_out_poll()` once a block (twice, at the start and after
-  your events, gets a message out sooner). Nothing waits for the wire:
-  the queue holds 32 messages, merges a newer controller value into a
-  waiting one, keeps room for note offs, and drops what doesn't fit,
-  never leaving a note hanging (`midi_out.h` has the rules).
-- Running status is used for you.
-- Thru is yours to do, if you want it: hand what `midi_read()` gives you
-  to `midi_out_send()`.
-**Raw bytes** (a System Exclusive message, a dump): from your serve,
-`midi_out_raw(buf, len)` streams them as they are, 12 bytes at a time
-whenever the wire is free; the buffer must stay as it is until
-`midi_out_raw_busy()` returns 0. Queued messages wait until the stream
-has gone, except realtime ones (a clock), which go out between its
-transfers so they keep their time. 4 096 bytes take 1.3 s of the wire;
-the queue fills meanwhile if you keep queueing, so send little else
-while a long stream runs.
-On the FM-1 itself these bytes reach no socket (it has no MIDI out
-jack); in the app, and on the boards that have one, they go out.

-#### The platform without the instrument (BR-2, R-PLAT-1)
-- **The platform's files:** boot (`crt0.S`, `start.c`), interrupts
-  (`irq.c`), the tick, the loop and the beacon (`main.c`), input
-  (`input.c`), audio (`audio.c`), the LCD and screen (`lcd.c`, `gfx.c`,
-  `font.c`, `screen.c`), MIDI in and out (`midi.c`, `midi_out.c`), the
-  store (`store.c`), and the test builds' `probe.c`. **The instrument's:**
-  `fm.c`, `fm_play.c`, `patches.c`, `arp.c`, `views.c`, `saving.c`,
-  `spectrum.c`, and for now `core1.S`, whose entry calls the FM engine's
-  core-1 loop (BR-3 makes core 1's start the platform's). `tools/build.sh`
-  lists them once (`INSTRUMENT`). Only `main.c` called the instrument,
-  and since BR-1 it doesn't when built with `SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL`; the
-  test builds' references are inside their own defines.
-- **`tools/build.sh build --platform`** leaves the instrument's files
-  out, defines `SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL` and links with
-  `firmware/platform.ld`; the engine comes from `--src` (BR-5). With
-  `--ld SCRIPT` an engine links with a script of its own (in the base or
-  in a `--src` folder) that includes the platform's (`INCLUDE
-  platform.ld`; the build passes `-L firmware`) and asserts its own
-  records; the package link uses the same script.
-- **The linker scripts.** `firmware/platform.ld` is what `app.ld` was,
-  less the instrument: the memory, the sections, the stacks and the
-  assertions about the platform's records. `firmware/app.ld` includes it
-  and asserts the instrument's records. The image is unchanged
-  (`da13d093…`); only the ELF's section names differ.
-- **Where an engine's records go.** The records sit at fixed addresses
-  that the tests (and the app) read, and the FM engine's record sits
-  between the audio record and MIDI's. A platform-only link would slide
-  MIDI's, MIDI out's and the store's records down by its size. So the
-  64 bytes there are now the **engine's slot** (`.beacon.engine0`,
-  `0x01C00590`): kept whether anything fills them or not (the script
-  moves the location counter past them), at most 64 bytes (more and the
-  link fails, as the counter would have to move back), the FM engine's
-  record in the base. After the store's record come the **engine's
-  records** (`.beacon.engine1` to `.beacon.engine4` in that order, then
-  `.beacon.engine`, from `0x01C00870`), as large as they need: the
-  base's interface record and arpeggiator's take the first two, so they
-  stay at `0x01C00870` and `0x01C008D0`; a firmware on the platform alone
-  gets `0x01C00870` for its first.
-- **Tested** (C-SEAMS, case platform): the test engine linked with the
-  platform alone and its own script (which asserts its record at
-  `0x01C00870`). The ELF holds none of the instrument's functions or
-  records, the platform's records are where the base has them, the
-  package link is built too, and the engine case's whole run passes on
-  it. The platform alone is 11 180 bytes of code (the firmware: 52 960).
-#### Core 1's start, the platform's (BR-3, R-CORE1-1)
-- **What.** Starting core 1 and handing it work were the FM engine's
-  (M5, "Two cores"): `core1.S`'s entry called the engine's loop on a
-  stack of its own, `fm_init()` pointed source 126's vector word at it
-  and set C1_CON bit 3 (HW-9), and `fm_play.c` kept the lock and the
-  shared loads (HW-65). The Plaits bench had its own copy of the entry
-  and the start. Now the platform has one of each (`core1.h`):
-  - `sb_core1_start(entry, stack_top)`: core 0 leaves the entry and the
-    stack's top where the entry (`core1_entry.S`) finds them, points the
-    vector word at it, sets the bit, and waits (`SB_CORE1_WAIT` polls,
-    about 1 ms in fwtest) for core 1 to say it runs; then puts the word
-    back and returns 1, or 0 if core 1 never said so. On core 1, the
-    entry sets both stack pointers from the given top and calls
-    `sb_core1_main` (`core1.c`), which says it runs, under the lock, and
-    calls the engine's entry; if that returns, core 1 stops with
-    interrupts off.
-  - `sb_lock`, `sb_unlock`, `sb_shared`, `sb_publish`: the lock byte
-    taken by test-and-set with csync around, a shared word read after
-    csync, a shared word written under a lock. `static inline`, as they
-    are short and sit in core 0's per-block path (the FM engine posts a
-    block and waits for its answer with them).
-- **The FM engine** keeps its own stack (1 KiB, as before, now a
-  `static` array in `fm_play.c`), its job's lock and sequence numbers,
-  and its loop; it starts core 1 with `sb_core1_start(fm_core1_main,
-  ...)` and keeps its two-core fallback (the result). Core 1's flag that
-  it runs is the platform's now, so `fm_core1_main` only sets
-  `sb_fm.core1`. **The Plaits bench** starts its core 1 the same way, on
-  its own 8 KiB stack, and its copy of the entry is gone.
-- **A name clash on the way.** The base names its objects by file name,
-  so `core1.c` and `core1.S` both made `core1.o` and the link failed
-  ("multiple definition"); the entry is `core1_entry.S`.
-- **The image changes** (code 53 028 bytes, from 52 960), and start-up
-  ends 2 to 3 µs later. One golden changed by hand, as the timing
-  goldens' policy says a change that is not a pure time shift must be:
-  midiout's MIDI capture, where the chord's three keys, pressed in the
-  same instant, now reach the engine in the order 60, 64, 67 (was 64, 67,
-  60); which key the panel's scan sees first depends on its phase
-  against the script, which the later start moved. Every other message
-  is the same, 2 to 3 µs later; the case's own checks take the chord in

-  later seam's image.
-- **Tested** (C-SEAMS, cases engine and platform): the test engine

-- **What moved.** M4b wrote a small runtime for the Plaits demo:
-  `memcpy`, `memmove` and `memset` (byte by byte), what C++ needs
-  (`__cxa_pure_virtual`, `operator delete`, each a halt if reached), the
-  soft-float routines, and freestanding headers (`<algorithm>`,
-  `<cmath>`, `<math.h>`, `<stddef.h>`, `<inttypes.h>`). They are now the
-  platform's, in `firmware/runtime/` (the headers in
-  `firmware/runtime/include/`), with a `<string.h>` declaring the three
-  `mem*` functions. Only `plaits_pre.h`, which is Plaits' own, stays
-  with the demo.
-- **An archive, so the firmware gets nothing it doesn't call.** The
-  build links every object it is given (no `--gc-sections`), so
-  `mem.c` as a plain object would add code to the firmware, which needs
-  none. The runtime is built into `libsb_runtime.a` (`ar` in its
-  deterministic mode) and the link takes it last: a member comes in only
-  when something calls it. The firmware calls none, so its image is the
-  same bytes; C-SEAMS checks build A has none of them. Its C is built
-  without the float instructions, as soft-float's must be (and as the
-  demo's C always was).

-#### SysEx bytes from MIDI in (BR-7, R-MIDI-8)
-- **What.** MIDI in's parser skipped System Exclusive, counting it (M6a).
-  A firmware built on the base may need its bytes (a dump of its own
-  data, for one, of a few kilobytes). `midi_sysex_tap(fn)` sets a
-  function the parser calls with each SysEx byte and what it is:
-  `MIDI_SYSEX_BEGIN` (the F0), `MIDI_SYSEX_DATA` (each data byte),
-  `MIDI_SYSEX_END` (the F7) or `MIDI_SYSEX_CUT` (any other status byte
-  that ends it: a new F0, a channel or system common status, or a
-  reset; the byte then also does what it always does). Realtime bytes
-  inside a SysEx (a clock, say) never reach the tap: they are messages
-  of their own, handed on by `midi_read()`, and the SysEx goes on after
-  them, as MIDI 1.0 has it. The parser is otherwise unchanged: its
-  counts, and `MIDI_SYSEX_LIMIT`, which only counts a message long, so a
-  message of any length reaches the tap whole.
-- **A tap, not pieces through `midi_read()`.** `midi_read()` hands on
-  whole messages of at most two data bytes, and the instrument and the
-  arpeggiator read it once a block; giving it SysEx in pieces would
-  change what every reader sees. A tap changes nothing for a firmware
-  that sets none (the base sets none), and costs one test of a pointer
-  per SysEx byte.
-- **Where it runs, and where the work goes.** The tap runs where the
-  parser runs: in `midi_read()`, from the engine's block callback, core
-  0's audio interrupt. So it should only keep the bytes (into a buffer
-  of the firmware's) and, at the end, add one to `sb_work` to wake
-  main; the work on them (checking, decoding, storing) goes in main's
-  loop, `sb_engine_serve()` (BR-1). At the wire's pace a block brings at
-  most five bytes, so the tap's share of a block is small whatever the
-  message's length; a 4 104-byte message takes 1.3 s to arrive.
-- **The image changes** (code 53 068 bytes, from 53 028): the pointer
-  tests in the parser.
-- **Tested** (C-SEAMS, case sysex) on the test engine linked with the
-  platform alone, which starts MIDI in and keeps each message's bytes
-  through the tap and sums them in its serve: a message of 4 104 data
-  bytes, with a clock byte in its middle, arrives whole and in order
-  (length, a sum weighted by place, first and last byte), the work done
-  in the serve; the clock is handed on as a message; a second message
-  cut short by a note on is reported cut by 0x90, and the note handed
-  on; MIDI's record counts the first long and drops nothing. The
-  firmware's own MIDI cases (C-FW-SUITE) check MIDI in is as before.
-#### Raw bytes to MIDI out (BR-8, R-MIDIOUT-9)
-- **What.** MIDI out sent queued messages of at most two data bytes
-  (M6b). `midi_out_raw(buf, len)` streams any bytes as they are (a
-  System Exclusive message, say): the poll hands the transmitter the
-  next transfer of up to `MIDI_OUT_CHUNK` (12) bytes whenever the last
-  has gone, as it does for messages. `midi_out_raw_busy()` says when the
-  last byte has been handed on and the buffer may change; a second call
-  meanwhile is refused (0).
-- **The queue waits, but for realtime.** A channel message inside a
-  System Exclusive message would end it, so the queue's messages wait
-  until the stream's last byte has been handed on. Realtime messages
-  (a clock, say) are the exception MIDI 1.0 makes: they may go anywhere,
-  even inside System Exclusive. So each transfer of a stream starts with
-  the realtime messages waiting, taken out of the queue (the others keep
-  their order), and a clock keeps its time through a long stream. The
-  stream may hold any status bytes, so the message after it carries its
-  status (running status starts again).
-- **The policy holds meanwhile.** Messages queued during a stream wait
-  under the same rules (merging, the reserve for note offs, dropping):
-  a stream of 4 096 bytes takes 1.3 s of the wire, longer than the
-  queue lasts at a busy rate, so a firmware that sends long streams
-  sends little else meanwhile, or accepts what the policy drops.
-- **Who calls it.** The queue is the block callback's alone (no lock).
-  The stream is handed over through three words the caller writes, the
-  last a sequence number the poll answers, so `midi_out_raw` may be
-  called from main's loop (`sb_engine_serve`, where the work on a SysEx
-  goes, BR-7) or from the block callback, as long as from one of them
-  only.
-- **Its counts** are in a record of their own (`sb_midi_out_raw`, found
-  by its symbol): MIDI out's record ends where the store's begins
-  (`0x01C00780`), so it can't grow.
-- **The image changes** (code 53 340 bytes, from 53 068).
-- **Tested** (C-SEAMS, case rawout) on the test engine linked with the
-  platform alone: at the first whole second its serve hands MIDI out a
-  600-byte System Exclusive message while its block callback queues a
-  clock every block and a note every 16th. On the wire: the 600 bytes in
-  order, nothing inside them but clocks (about 200), every note after
-  the F7, the first with its status, and every clock and note sent. The
-  firmware's own MIDI out cases (C-FW-SUITE) check MIDI out is as before.
-#### Storage for large records (BR-9, R-STORE-10)
-- **What.** The store kept the base's own records: a patch (112 bytes)
-  in each of 16 slots, the selection, the settings, a reset. A firmware
-  built on the base needs its own, some large (a payload of 4 096 bytes,
-  say). Kinds 0x80 to 0xFE are now kept for firmwares built on the base,
-  with any id, and `store_put`/`store_get` take a payload of up to 5 904
-  bytes for them (docs/STORE-FORMAT.md, "Kinds for firmwares built on
-  the base"). A reset voids them with everything else.
-- **Why parts.** A sector is 4 KiB with a 16-byte header, and a record
-  can't leave its sector, so a 4 096-byte payload can't be one record. It
-  is written as parts, records of up to 492 bytes of it (512 with their
-  header, tag and CRC), each carrying its index and the part count in
-  the header's two bytes that were always 0, and a tag (the write's own
-  number) as its payload's first word. Of each part the newest record
-  counts, as for any key; the payload is read only when every part is
-  there with part 0's tag and count. A write never mixes with the one
-  before it: cut short, the old payload still reads until the new
-  write's first part is whole, and then nothing until its last part is
-  (the model checks every cut point: old, then none, then new; fwtest's
-  power cut checks one on the firmware). A firmware that can't do without
-  its payload writes it again; the store never hands it half of each.
-- **Why not keep the old one through the whole write.** That needs room
-  for two copies of the payload at once, and the three sectors don't
-  have it: the ring needs a sector's worth free to move on, so about two
-  sectors (8 160 bytes) hold everything live, and two copies of 4 096
-  bytes are 8 192 before any header. Writing part by part needs room for
-  one new part beside everything live.
-- **What today's region holds** (`tools/store.py`'s model, which the
-  firmware's images match after every run of the seams suite): one
-  payload of up to 5 396 bytes, rewritten as often as asked, with
-  nothing else stored (a firmware on the platform alone, its own small
-  records aside); a 4 096-byte payload so has 1.3 KB to spare. Beside the
-  base's full store (all 16 user slots, the selection and the settings,
-  saved between rewrites) how much fits depends on how the records fall
-  in the sectors: 2 952 bytes held in every one of 40 histories of 300
-  rewrites the model tried; up to about 3.5 KB in some histories but not
-  all; 4 096 not reliably. Past what fits a write is refused
-  (`STORE_ERR_FULL`), and what was there stays. Where a larger region
-  goes is the owner's later decision; the part size was chosen for
-  today's: of the sizes tried, from 236 to 2 012 bytes, 492 let the most
-  be rewritten beside the base's full store (428 a little more alone).
-- **Keys.** The base's keys are fixed (16 slots and three more). The
-  firmware kinds' parts take places in a table of their own, 32 of them,
-  after the base's: the ring's compaction, a sector's live count and the
-  reset treat both alike, in that order, and the model keeps the same
-  order, so an image it writes is one the firmware could have written.
-  A write checks first that every part has a place, so it never stops
-  for want of one; a payload rewritten with fewer parts frees the rest.
-- **Format.** Version 1's records, as before: a reader that doesn't know
-  these kinds (the base before this) counts them unknown and never
-  copies them forward. The base's own records and their limits are
-  unchanged, and its tests pass as they are.
-- **The image changes** (code 54 416 bytes, from 53 340; RAM 1 312 bytes
-  more: the table, and the record buffers sized for a part).
-- **Tested:** the model in C-UNIT (a payload in parts read whole, every
-  cut point of a rewrite, fewer parts, the reset, what the region holds,
-  the constants the firmware's); and the firmware in C-SEAMS (case
-  store): nine runs chained through the flash file, the model writing a
-  control record before each that tells the test engine what to do: a
-  4 096-byte payload and a small one written and read back, then read at
-  the next start-up; rewritten; rewritten again with the power cut at
-  the middle of its page programs, after which the large payload is gone
-  and the small one stays; rewritten after the cut; a reset voids both;
-  then alone, 5 000 bytes written and read back and 5 904 refused as
-  full. The model reads what the firmware does after every run.

lines: Embedded audio experiments. Work in progress.
MIT licensed (see `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`). How changes are made and recorded:
-`CONTRIBUTING.md`. What is planned: `docs/PLAN.md`.
+`CONTRIBUTING.md`. What is planned: `docs/PLAN.md`. Building your own on
+this base: `docs/BUILDING-ON-SMALL-BEEPS.md`.
## Build
+SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
+SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
+# Building your own firmware on small-beeps
+small-beeps is a base: a platform that starts the chip and runs the
+panel, the screen, the audio output, MIDI in and out and the flash store,
+plus an FM instrument that uses it. You can keep the platform as it is and
+put your own engine where the instrument was, in your own repository,
+without changing a file of the base. This guide shows how, from an empty
+repository to a firmware running in fwtest and in the F-Emulator app.
+Everything here is MIT-licensed, like the rest of small-beeps: keep its
+`LICENSE` and `NOTICE` with your copy. The seams this guide uses are
+described in more depth in docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, "Seams for firmwares
+built on small-beeps", and their requirements are in docs/REQUIREMENTS.md
+(R-ENG-1, R-PLAT-1, R-CORE1-1, R-RT-1, R-MIDI-8, R-MIDIOUT-9, R-STORE-10,
+R-BUILD-3, R-BUILD-4).
+## 1. Set up
+You need git, Docker (any host; the build and the tests run as
+linux/amd64 containers) and Python 3.9 or later.
+mkdir my-firmware && cd my-firmware && git init
+git submodule add https://github.com/japes98/small-beeps base
+mkdir src
+sh base/tools/build.sh image      # once: the pinned build image, made locally
+`build.sh image` builds the base's build image on your machine: a pinned
+Debian with the chip's toolchain, downloaded from its vendor and checked
+against its SHA-256 (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md). The image and the toolchain are
+never published anywhere; keep them out of your repository too.
+Your repository then holds `base/` (the base, unmodified, at a commit you
+choose) and `src/` (your sources). Everything below runs from your
+repository's root.
+## 2. Write your engine
+Your engine is three functions (`base/firmware/src/engine.h`):
+#include "audio.h"
+#include "engine.h"
+#include "input.h"
+#include "midi.h"
+#include "midi_out.h"
+void sb_engine_init(void)
+    midi_settings_default(&midi_settings);   /* MIDI's settings: out on channel 1, ... */
+    midi_start();                            /* the UART, for MIDI in and out */
+void sb_engine_block(s32 *out, u32 frames)
+    struct input_event e;
+    struct midi_msg m;
+    while (input_read_audio(&e))
+        ;                                    /* the panel's events: keys, encoders, the pot */
+    midi_poll();
+    while (midi_read(&m))
+        ;                                    /* MIDI in's messages */
+    for (n = 0; n < frames; n++)
+        out[2 * n] = out[2 * n + 1] = 0;     /* your sound: 24-bit, left then right */
+    midi_out_poll();                         /* send what you queued */
+void sb_engine_serve(void)
+    /* slow work: the screen, the store, a SysEx you received */
+| Function | When | Where it runs |
+| `sb_engine_init` | once, at start-up, before interrupts are on and the audio starts | core 0, main |
+| `sb_engine_block` | every audio block: `AUDIO_FRAMES` (64) stereo frames, 1.45 ms | core 0, the audio interrupt |
+| `sb_engine_serve` | once before main's loop, then whenever something added work | core 0, main's loop |
+- **The block callback must keep up**: a block is 1.45 ms of core 0's
+  time, shared with the tick and the panel's scan. Do the sound and the
+  quick reactions here, nothing that waits.
+- **Waking main.** Main sleeps between interrupts and calls your serve
+  when `sb_work` (`sb.h`) changed: the tick adds one each whole second,
+  the panel's scan one per event. Add one yourself (`sb_work++`) from the
+  block callback when you leave main work, as a finished SysEx message.
+- **The screen.** Main brings the screen up and shows a test screen with
+  a heartbeat. To draw your own, set `sb_beacon.screen` to another value
+  (`SB_SCREEN_PANEL`, `sb.h`), so main stops drawing the heartbeat, then
+  draw into the frame buffer with `gfx_*` and send rows with
+  `lcd_send_rows()` or a rectangle with `lcd_send_rect()` (`sb.h`; wait
+  for `lcd_busy()` to be 0 first), from your serve.
+- **C++** works too: name the file `.cc`. The platform's runtime has
+  `memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset`, `<algorithm>`, `<string.h>`,
+  `<inttypes.h>`, `<stddef.h>`, `<math.h>` and what virtual classes and
+  static objects need (`base/firmware/runtime/`); there is no heap, no
+  exceptions and no RTTI. Static objects' constructors run before your
+  init.
+## 3. What the platform gives you
+All from `base/firmware/src/`, all yours to call:
+| Part | Header | What |
+| The panel | `input.h` | events (`input_read_audio` in the block callback, `input_read` in main), each control's value (`input_value`), the LEDs (`input_led`) |
+| Audio | `audio.h` | the block size and rate; your block callback fills the buffer |
+| The screen | `sb.h` | `gfx_fill`, `gfx_text`, `gfx_line`, ...; `lcd_send_rows`, `lcd_send_rect`, `lcd_busy` |
+| MIDI in | `midi.h` | `midi_start`, `midi_poll` and `midi_read` (whole messages, from the block callback); `midi_sysex_tap` (System Exclusive's bytes, below) |
+| MIDI out | `midi_out.h` | below, section 7 |
+| The store | `store.h` | `store_init` (once, in your init), `store_get`, `store_put`, `store_reset`, below |
+| Core 1 | `core1.h` | `sb_core1_start(entry, stack_top)`; `sb_lock`, `sb_unlock`, `sb_shared`, `sb_publish` to hand it work |
+| Time | `sb.h` | `sb_now()` (24 MHz), `sb_ticks()`, `sb_wait_ms()` (main only), the heartbeat in `sb_beacon` |
+**System Exclusive in.** `midi_sysex_tap(fn)` sets a function MIDI in's
+parser calls for each byte of a System Exclusive message:
+`MIDI_SYSEX_BEGIN`, each `MIDI_SYSEX_DATA` byte, then `MIDI_SYSEX_END` or
+`MIDI_SYSEX_CUT`. It runs in the block callback: keep the bytes in a
+buffer of your own and, at the end, add one to `sb_work`; work on them in
+your serve. Messages of any length come through (tested with 4 104 data
+bytes).
+**The store.** Kinds `0x80` to `0xFE` are yours, any id from 0 to 255,
+and a payload of up to 5 904 bytes each (`STORE_FW_MAX`):
+store_init();                                     /* in your init */
+n = store_get(0x80, 0, buf, sizeof buf, &version);  /* -1: none */
+r = store_put(0x80, 0, 1, buf, len);              /* from your serve: it waits for the flash */
+A payload is read whole or not at all: if the power goes during a write,
+the old one is still there until the new write's first part is written,
+and then there is none until you write it again. Write from your serve,
+never from the block callback (a write takes the flash for some
+milliseconds). The store's region today is three sectors (12 KiB): with
+nothing else in it, it holds and rewrites one payload of up to 5 396
+bytes; `store_put` returns `STORE_ERR_FULL` past what fits, and what was
+there stays. `store_reset()` voids everything (a factory reset).
+docs/STORE-FORMAT.md has the bytes.
+## 4. Your records in RAM
+Tests read state at fixed RAM addresses. The platform keeps its records
+at the start of RAM (`base/firmware/platform.ld`) and keeps two places
+for an engine's:
+- the engine's slot, `0x01C00590`: one record of at most 64 bytes, in
+  section `.beacon.engine0`;
+- after the store's record, from `0x01C00870`: sections
+  `.beacon.engine1` to `.beacon.engine4`, then `.beacon.engine`, in that
+  order, any size.
+volatile struct my_record my_record __attribute__((section(".beacon.engine1")));
+Write a linker script of your own that includes the platform's and
+asserts where your records landed, so a change shows at link time:
+/* src/my.ld */
+INCLUDE platform.ld
+ASSERT(my_record == 0x01C00870, "my record must follow the store's")
+## 5. Build
+sh base/tools/build.sh build --out out --platform --src src --ld src/my.ld
+| Option | What |
+| `--platform` | leaves out the base's instrument (its FM engine, presets, arpeggiator, screens and saving), builds with `SB_ENGINE_EXTERNAL`, links with `platform.ld` |
+| `--src DIR` | every `.c`, `.S` and `.cc` under DIR, built with the firmware's flags and `-I DIR`; repeat it for more folders (not a folder holding `base/`) |
+| `--ld SCRIPT` | your linker script (in `base/` or in a `--src` folder) |
+| `--define NAME` | `-DNAME` for every source (yours and the base's) |
+| `--leave-out FILE` | a base source left out (`firmware/src/...`), to replace it with your own |
+The outputs, in `out/`:
+- `app.bin`: the raw image (linked at `0x02000000`), what fwtest and the
+  app run;
+- `app-pkg.bin`: the same code linked at `0x02000120`, for a `.fwsc`
+  package (section 6);
+- `app.elf`, `app-pkg.elf`: with symbols, for finding things;
+- `app.size`: code, data, RAM and stack in bytes;
+- `SHA256SUMS`.
+The build is deterministic: the same sources give the same bytes, from
+any folder on any machine. It refuses an object holding a store that
+writes back into its own base register (`[++rN=k] = rN`, ...), as what
+the chip does then is still open (R-BUILD-3); if your code trips it, the
+message names the file, the function and the instruction.
+## 6. Test with fwtest, run in the app
+**fwtest** runs your image in an emulator of the chip, from its pinned
+container image: keys, encoders, the pot and MIDI in from a script; the
+screen, the audio, MIDI out, RAM and the flash chip out.
+sh base/tools/fwtest run out/app.bin --ms 3000 --out out/t1 \
+    --script tests/keys.txt --wav --midi-out --lcd 2500 \
+Paths must be inside the folder you run it from (your repository's
+root). docs/HARNESS.md (`base/docs/HARNESS.md`) is its manual: the script
+format, every output, the flash chip's timing and power cuts
+(`--flash`, `--flash-out`, `--power-cut`), golden files and suites. The
+base's own tests of these seams are a working example:
+`base/tools/seams_suite.py` with its test engine in
+`base/tests/seams/engine/`.
+**The F-Emulator app** runs the same image:
+- the bare image: open `out/app.bin` in the app;
+- or a package: pack the package link into a `.fwsc` and check it with
+  the reader fwtest also uses:
+  python3 base/tools/fwsc.py pack out/app-pkg.bin --version 0.1.0 \
+      --identity my-firmware-0.1.0 --out out/my-firmware.fwsc
+  python3 base/tools/fwsc.py out/my-firmware.fwsc

+## 7. MIDI out
+**What the base sends for you:** nothing, once you build with
+`--platform`. The base's instrument sends the panel's notes, knobs and
+program changes, passes MIDI thru and sends the arpeggiator's clock; all
+of that is the instrument's, and goes with it. The platform only sends
+what your engine queues.
+**Sending your own:**
+- Call `midi_start()` in your init (it turns the UART on for both
+  directions) and `midi_settings_default(&midi_settings)` (the out
+  channel, 1, comes from there).
+- From the block callback, queue messages with `midi_out_channel(kind,
+  d1, d2)` (on the out channel) or `midi_out_send(&msg)` (any status),
+  and call `midi_out_poll()` once a block (twice, at the start and after
+  your events, gets a message out sooner). Nothing waits for the wire:
+  the queue holds 32 messages, merges a newer controller value into a
+  waiting one, keeps room for note offs, and drops what doesn't fit,
+  never leaving a note hanging (`midi_out.h` has the rules).
+- Running status is used for you.
+- Thru is yours to do, if you want it: hand what `midi_read()` gives you
+  to `midi_out_send()`.
+**Raw bytes** (a System Exclusive message, a dump): from your serve,
+`midi_out_raw(buf, len)` streams them as they are, 12 bytes at a time
+whenever the wire is free; the buffer must stay as it is until
+`midi_out_raw_busy()` returns 0. Queued messages wait until the stream
+has gone, except realtime ones (a clock), which go out between its
+transfers so they keep their time. 4 096 bytes take 1.3 s of the wire;
+the queue fills meanwhile if you keep queueing, so send little else
+while a long stream runs.
+On the FM-1 itself these bytes reach no socket (it has no MIDI out
+jack); in the app, and on the boards that have one, they go out.
+## 8. Keeping up with the base
+Move `base/` to a newer commit when you want its fixes
+(`git -C base pull`, then commit the submodule). The seams are meant to
+stay as they are; a change to one is noted in docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md and
+its requirement. Run your tests again after each update: the build and
+fwtest are pinned by the base, so a result changes only when the base or
+your code does.
